6 Evaluate and iterateMonitor outcomes and keep policies relevant

A cooperative bank, as an illustration. It plans to open 20 rural branches in two years.

  1. Vision: reach farmers and small traders who now travel to town to bank.
  2. Measures: accounts opened per branch, loan repayment, and staff turnover in rural branches.
  3. Readiness: few current staff know crop loans or speak the local language.
  4. Forecast: 20 branches × 6 staff = 120 people. If 40 can transfer, 120 − 40 = 80 must be hired or trained.
  5. Systems: the HR software cannot handle transfers across districts, so it is upgraded.
  6. Evaluate: six months in, rural branches are losing staff fastest, so the bank revises its posting allowance.

Strategic HR planning runs in five steps:

  1. Define SMART goals: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
  2. Assess HR capabilities.
  3. Evaluate workforce skills.
  4. Analyse departmental needs.
  5. Recruit strategically, for cultural fit, adaptability and future readiness.

Don't confuse people analytics with HR reporting. Reporting counts what happened: headcount, attrition, days to hire. Analytics asks why it happened and what is likely next, such as which new hires are at risk of leaving.

Where it breaks. Data reduce bias only when the data are sound. A hiring model built on a firm's past choices can repeat the bias in those choices. The steps also look neater on paper than in life; firms often loop back before reaching step 6.

For exams. Know the six steps in order, and the five steps of strategic HR planning, starting with SMART goals. Step 6, evaluate and iterate, is the one that makes SHRM continuous.

The right people, with the right capabilities, for the right strategy, at the right time.

text: The Kuṟaḷ tells the ruler to look every day into the conduct of those who do his work: if they do not swerve, the world will not swerve. SHRM's last step, evaluating and iterating, is the same discipline of regular review.
pairings.quote: “Let the ruler look daily into the conduct of those who work for him; if they do not swerve, the world will not swerve.” நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான் கோடாமை கோடா துலகு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 520

chapters.title: Competency Mapping and the Balanced Scorecard
chapters.scope: What a competency is, how organisations map the competencies each job needs, and how the balanced scorecard places people measures within strategy.

blocks.title: Competency and its types
blocks.html:
Two clerks in a public-sector bank branch have the same degree and the same years of service. One stays calm with an angry customer and spots posting errors early; the other does not. Qualifications cannot explain the gap. Competencies can.

In plain wordsA competency is a mix of what a person knows, can do and is like that shows up as good performance in a role.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a competency is a demonstrable individual characteristic that enables effective job performance. It is often built from four parts: knowledge, skills, attitudes and traits.

PartMeaningBank clerk example
KnowledgeWhat a person knowsThe rules for opening and closing accounts
SkillsWhat a person can doPosting entries quickly and accurately
AttitudesThe outlook a person brings to the workTreating a customer's problem as one's own
TraitsEnduring personal qualitiesStaying calm under pressure

Knowledge and skills are the easiest parts to train and to test. Attitudes and traits are harder to see and slower to change, so employers often select for them and train for the rest.

Three types. Competencies are sorted by how widely a job family needs them.

TypeWho needs itExamplesWhat it gives the organisation
CoreEveryone; tied to what the organisation is trying to achieveDecision-making, teamwork, adaptability, communication, integrityA common standard of behaviour that supports the strategy
Cross-functionalMany jobs in many departmentsComputer skills, budgetingVersatile staff, lower training cost, faster collaboration, more loyalty
Functional (technical)One job or job familyData analysis, risk assessment, software developmentTask proficiency and specialisation

At a Pune auto-parts plant, as an illustration: every employee needs integrity and teamwork (core). Supervisors, planners and stores staff all need to read a budget (cross-functional). Only the tool-room staff need to programme a CNC machine (functional).

Don't confuse these "core competencies" with a firm's core competence. In strategy, a core competence (Prahalad and Hamel, 1990) is a collective strength of the whole firm that rivals find hard to copy. In this HR sense, "core" means the behaviours every employee needs. Some textbooks use a different split altogether: technical, behavioural and managerial competencies. Learn the scheme your own text uses, and know that the other exists.

Where it breaks. Generic words like "teamwork" or "integrity" appear on almost every firm's list. They help only once each is written as behaviour you can observe, such as "shares information with the next shift without being asked". Traits and attitudes can also be measured only through behaviour, which invites bias.

For exams. Know the four parts, the three types with two examples each, and the idea that a competency is something demonstrable. The next block shows how organisations identify and record competencies job by job.

Know, can do, outlook, trait: and three reaches, core, cross-functional, functional.

blocks.title: The competency mapping process
blocks.html:
A firm wants to promote its best technician to supervisor, hire a new planner and train the stores team. Each decision needs the same answer: what does this job demand, in behaviour you can see? Mapping works that out once and reuses it.

In plain wordsCompetency mapping is deciding which competencies each job needs, writing them down, and using them in hiring, training, appraisal and promotion.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: competency mapping is the process of identifying the key competencies for an organisation and for each job, and building them into HR processes such as recruitment, training, appraisal and promotion. It links roles to performance expectations and to business goals.

Why organisations do it.

  • Staff are costly, so a wrong hire or an early exit is expensive.
  • People are an asset, and the right people can run technology, finance, markets and customer relationships well.
  • Getting more from people beats getting more people: mapping shows who can be upskilled.
  • Customers expect more, so service competencies must be built on purpose.

The four stages.

StageWhat happens
1 Design the questionnaireFix the job's purpose. Find its critical success factors (the few things that must go right) and its key result areas (the outcomes it is judged on). Break each result area into key activities.
2 Collect the dataGet clarity on the organisation's direction and structure. Interview the jobholder and the jobholder's reporting officer. Hold a focus group when several jobs belong to one family.
3 Analyse and mapRank-order the competencies. Compare good performers with average ones. Check the list against research or industry data. Assign competencies to positions.
4 FinaliseWrite the role descriptions and the competency set for each job, with measurable indicators.

Back to the plant, as an illustration, for a stores supervisor. The purpose is to keep every line supplied. A critical success factor is no stock-outs. A key result area is stock accuracy, and one key activity is a weekly bin count. In stage 3 the analyst finds that the best supervisors check bin counts against the records every day, and average ones do so only before audits. "Attention to detail" ranks high. In stage 4 it is written as an indicator: reconciles bin counts with records daily and reports gaps the same day.

Don't confuse the four stages with the five-step programme. The stages build the map for a job. Study materials also give a five-step sequence for rolling a map out across an organisation:

  1. Leaders agree the core competencies needed for the organisation's goals.
  2. HR assesses what level of each competency each type of position needs, usually by interviewing sample jobholders.
  3. Job descriptions are rewritten with the competencies, and the same competencies enter the appraisal form.
  4. A competency matrix shows career paths as competencies grow in sophistication.
  5. HR and each employee draw up an individual development plan: courses, workshops, mentoring.

Mapping also differs from job analysis. Job analysis records the tasks and duties of a job (see the Job analysis chapter). Mapping asks what behaviour separates strong performers in it. Job analysis is often an input to mapping.

Where it breaks. A map takes time to build and goes stale when jobs change. Copying what today's top performers do may also copy their bad habits, and may miss what the job will need next year. Interview data depends on how honestly and how well people describe their own work.

In practice. A finished map is reused four ways: to write selection criteria, to find training gaps, to appraise on the same criteria, and to choose people for promotion. That reuse is the point of mapping.

For exams. Expect the four stages in order, with what each involves, and the uses: recruitment, training, appraisal and promotion.

Design, collect, analyse, finalise.

blocks.title: Methods of competency mapping
blocks.html:
A bank branch must choose one relationship manager from forty applicants, and a manufacturer must write competency sets for four thousand employees. The first needs a method that watches people act; the second needs one that reaches many people cheaply. No single method serves both, so mapping draws on five.

In plain wordsA mapping method is a way of collecting evidence about what a job demands or who can meet it.

MethodHow it worksStrengthWatch out for
Assessment centreCandidates work through simulations, such as group discussion, in-basket exercise, role-play and case analysis, while trained assessors observeShows behaviour under realistic pressure; usually regarded as a good predictor of later performanceCostly and slow; needs trained assessors
Critical incident techniqueCollect real examples of exceptionally good or poor performance soon after they happen, then group them by behaviourLinks competencies to real events, not opinionShows the extremes, not the ordinary day
InterviewsOne-to-one conversation, structured or semi-structured, on experience, motivation, values and cultural fitFirst-hand insight; answers can be compared with the mapDepends on the interviewer's questions and bias
QuestionnairesStandard forms that describe work activities and requirementsReaches many people cheaplyDescribes the job more than the person; generic forms can miss local detail
Psychometric testsStandardised tests of aptitude or achievementConsistent and objective measure of a sample of attributesA sample, not the whole person; must be valid for the job

Assessment centre and critical incidents. An assessment "centre" is a method, not a building. The critical incident technique is credited to John Flanagan (1954) and also appears as a job analysis method.

Questionnaires. Several standard instruments are used. The Common Metric Questionnaire (CMQ) records work requirements and activities. The Position Analysis Questionnaire (PAQ) links job characteristics to human characteristics. The Occupational Analysis Inventory lists work elements across many occupations, and the Work Profiling System covers ability and personality attributes. Functional Job Analysis (FJA) is often listed here too, but it is a job analysis method developed by Sidney Fine, not a form. It rates what a worker does in relation to data, people and things.

Psychometric tests are of two kinds. An aptitude test shows natural inclination, such as for numbers or design, and predicts how well a person will learn with training. An achievement test shows what a person has already learned, such as in mathematics or language.

Don't confuse job analysis tools with competency methods. CMQ, PAQ and FJA come from job analysis. They describe work in a way that can be turned into required competencies, so mapping borrows them, but they do not assess a person. Likewise, aptitude means "can learn"; achievement means "has learned".

Where it breaks. Each method has a blind spot, so careful mapping combines two or three. An interview alone can favour the confident talker; a test alone cannot show how a person behaves in a team.

For exams. Expect to name the five methods and match each to its description, and to tell aptitude from achievement tests. When CMQ, PAQ or FJA appear, remember they belong to job analysis.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. You must map the competencies of customer-service agents in a firm with 3,000 of them, and select 12 team leaders from 60 internal candidates. Use a questionnaire and a few interviews for the first, because breadth matters and the stakes for each person are low. For the second, an assessment centre with a role-play and an in-basket is worth its cost: 12 promotions shape the team for years. A critical incident exercise run with the best and weakest agents can sharpen the first map cheaply.

Triangulation. When two methods agree, trust the finding more. When they disagree, treat that as a question: a candidate who tests well but performs poorly in simulation may know the theory without having the habit.

Centre, incidents, interviews, questionnaires, tests.

blocks.title: The balanced scorecard and people measures
blocks.html:
A plant reports a record profit, but its best technicians are leaving and deliveries are slipping. Profit reports the past, so it is the last number to show trouble. A manager who watches only money learns of the problem too late.

In plain wordsThe balanced scorecard measures an organisation from four sides (money, customers, internal processes, and learning and growth) so that profit is not the only test.

Exam definitionThe balanced scorecard is a strategic performance-measurement system introduced by Robert Kaplan and David Norton (Harvard Business Review, 1992) that turns an organisation's mission and strategy into objectives and measures in four perspectives.

It is a framework for the whole organisation, not a tool for HR alone. Its balance is between financial and non-financial measures, and between results that have already happened and the drivers of future results. Unit 6 (Strategy implementation and evaluation) sets out the four perspectives and their questions. This block looks at where people measures sit in them.

PerspectiveHow people affect itExample people measures (illustrations)
FinancialPeople deliver the results and are also the main costRevenue per employee; people cost as a share of revenue
CustomerStaff are what the customer meetsCustomer satisfaction for service teams; repeat customers
Internal business processSkill and discipline decide how well work flowsError rate; order cycle time; time taken to fill a vacancy
Learning and growthSkills, motivation, tools and culture decide whether the other three can keep improvingShare of staff meeting the competency standard for their role; engagement score; retention of key staff; ideas put into use

Link to competency mapping. The competency map supplies the yardstick for learning and growth. Suppose the map says a stores supervisor needs "attention to detail" at a given level. The scorecard can track how many supervisors reach it. It can also test whether closing that gap improves stock accuracy, an internal process measure.

Don't confuse learning and growth with customer retention. Customer retention belongs to the Customer perspective. Learning and growth is about the organisation's own capability: employee skills and training, information systems, and culture. Study notes also sometimes call the scorecard a tool "for evaluating HRM" or list "Human Resource" as a fifth perspective. It is a general strategic framework, and the four perspectives are the whole list. Names vary slightly between books: Financial (or Finance), Customer, Internal Business Process (or Business Processes), Learning and Growth.

Where it breaks. People measures are the hardest to choose well. Training hours show effort, not skill gained. Engagement and retention move slowly and have many causes, so linking them to profit is a matter of judgement. As with any scorecard, staff may work to the measure and not to its purpose, and too many measures blur the focus.

For exams. Know Kaplan and Norton (1992), the four perspectives and a measure for each. Learning and growth covers people and capability; the chain of cause and effect runs from it up to financial results.

Go deeper for practitioners

Leading measures. Financial results lag. Skills, engagement and process quality move first. If key staff retention drops this quarter, profit per employee is unlikely to hold for long.

Employee outcomes. In their later book (1996), Kaplan and Norton treat employee satisfaction, retention and productivity as core outcome measures of learning and growth, driven by enablers such as staff competencies, technology and the climate for action.

The HR scorecard. Becker, Huselid and Ulrich (2001) adapted the idea to the HR function itself, so HR can show how its practices support the strategy. This is the HR-specific tool; the original scorecard is not.

A decision. A branch network raised training hours sharply, yet complaints did not fall. Ask whether the training addressed the competencies the map says matter for the complaint-prone roles. If not, the measure was counting hours, not capability.

Money, customers, processes, learning: people at the foundation.

chapters.title: Performance Management and Appraisal
chapters.scope: How organisations manage and judge performance: the five-phase cycle, the traditional and modern methods of appraisal, rater errors, and how to make appraisal fair.

blocks.title: Performance management and its cycle
blocks.html:
An operator at a Pune auto-parts plant hears at his April review that his rejects were too high all last year. Nobody told him in June, when he could still have fixed it. Performance management exists so that the review is never the first time he hears.

In plain wordsPerformance management is the year-round routine of agreeing what good work looks like, watching it, helping people reach it, and rewarding them when they do.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: performance management is a continuous, strategic process of improving individual and organisational performance by aligning employees' work with organisational goals, through ongoing communication and feedback between manager and employee.

Performance appraisal is one event inside that routine: a formal, periodic evaluation of how well a person did in the period just ended, usually once or twice a year.

Point of differencePerformance managementPerformance appraisal
NatureOngoing and developmentalA formal evaluation
Time focusLooks ahead: how to improveLooks back at past performance
TimingAll year: plan, monitor, feedback, review, developUsually annual or half-yearly
ScopeA strategic system linking work to the organisation's goalsOne step of that system

Objectives of performance management. There are four:

  • Goal alignment: directing each person's effort towards the organisation's strategic outcomes.
  • Continuous improvement: building a high-performance culture through regular feedback and coaching.
  • Employee development: finding skill gaps, training needs and growth opportunities.
  • Recognition and motivation: raising morale through rewards, bonuses and recognition, such as an Employee of the Month award.

The five-phase cycle. The phases repeat, and what the last one learns feeds the next round of planning.

PhaseWhat happensAt the plant (an illustration)
1 Performance planningManager and employee set SMART goals: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-boundKeep rejects below 2% of parts made, by March
2 Performance monitoringTrack progress against KPIs and checkpointsThe supervisor reads the weekly reject count
3 Feedback and coachingTimely, constructive feedback so people correct course earlyIn June, a senior fitter shows him a better set-up
4 Performance review (appraisal)Formal evaluation against the goals and against competencies, the skills and behaviours the job needsThe year-end rating and discussion
5 Rewards and developmentLink results to rewards, promotion or trainingA bonus, and a place on a machine-setting course

Four key terms run through the cycle.

TermMeaningAt the plant
Key performance indicator (KPI)A specific, measurable figure used to track performancePercentage of parts rejected
Performance standardThe level of performance expectedNo more than 2% rejects
Performance gapThe difference between expected and actual performance5% rejects against 2% allowed
Performance improvement plan (PIP)A structured, time-limited plan to bring an underperformer up to standardThree months of coaching, with a check every two weeks

The gap, worked. The fitter makes 5,000 parts. The standard allows 2%, which is 100 rejects. He has 5%, which is 250 rejects. The gap is 250 − 100 = 150 parts, or 3 percentage points. A good plan tackles why: the set-up, the tool wear, or his skill. Measures like KPIs are often grouped under four headings (financial, customer, internal process, learning and growth) in the Balanced Scorecard, which has its own chapter.

Don't confuse performance management with performance appraisal. Appraisal is the formal look back; management is the whole year of planning, watching, helping and rewarding. Textbooks also name the five phases as planning, monitoring, developing, rating and rewarding. It is the same loop with different labels.

Where it breaks. On paper the cycle is tidy; in practice, managers often skip the middle phases, and it shrinks to a form filled in once a year. A KPI also tends to steer behaviour: if only rejects are counted, speed or teamwork may suffer.

In practice. Standards come from the job description, which comes from job analysis. The gap tells the manager whether the fix is training, tools or something else.

For exams. Know the contrast in the first table, the five phases in order, and the four key terms. SMART is a favourite.

Plan, monitor, feedback, review, reward: then plan again.

blocks.title: Traditional appraisal methods
blocks.html:
A bank branch manager must name the best of twelve clerks by Friday. If she lines them up from best to worst, she gets one answer; if she scores each one on punctuality and teamwork, she may get another. The method decides what she sees.

In plain wordsA traditional appraisal method judges a person by comparing them with co-workers or by scoring them on a list of traits, mostly looking back at the past period.

Exam definitionA standard textbook grouping: the traditional methods are ranking, paired comparison, graphic rating scale, checklist, critical incident and confidential report. The modern methods (next block) look more at results, behaviour and potential.

MethodHow it worksStrengthWeakness
RankingThe rater puts employees in order, from best to worstSimple to run and explainNo detail: it does not say why one is better, or by how much
Paired comparisonEach employee is compared with every other, one pair at a time; the one with most "wins" ranks firstMore careful than rankingThe number of pairs grows fast in a large team
Graphic rating scaleThe rater scores traits such as punctuality, initiative and teamwork on a scale, say from poor to excellent, and the scores are addedCheap, easy, fits every jobTraits are vague, so rater bias creeps in
ChecklistThe rater ticks yes or no against a list of statements; the HR department does the scoringEasy to use, standard for allLittle depth; the HR weights may be poor
Critical incidentThe supervisor records specific examples of very good or very poor behaviour through the periodBased on real behaviour; gives rich feedbackNeeds steady record-keeping; can feel like fault-finding
Confidential reportThe superior writes a private report on conduct, strengths and weaknessesFamiliar in government and public-sector bodiesSubjective and not transparent

Paired comparison, counted. With N employees, the number of pairs is N × (N − 1) ÷ 2. For the six clerks it is 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 comparisons. For twelve it is 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66. The clerk who wins the most pairs ranks first.

Confidential report. In its classic form, as in the Annual Confidential Report of government service, the employee does not see the report. Feedback comes only if there is an adverse entry. Ratings are tied to promotion, so they are open to manipulation. Many government services have moved towards open reports that the officer sees.

Other traditional methods. Textbooks list several more:

  • Forced distribution: the rater must spread employees across the scale in fixed shares, on the assumption that performance follows a bell curve. It stops everyone being rated high, but it is unfair to a strong team.
  • Forced choice: the rater picks, from sets of statements, the one that fits best. Which statements count for more is hidden from the rater, so favouritism has less room.
  • Essay method: the rater writes a free description of strengths, weaknesses and promotion potential. It fills gaps a checklist leaves, but depends on the rater's writing and memory.
  • Field review: someone from outside the department, often from HR, reviews the employee. It gives comparable ratings for promotion, but the reviewer does not see the daily work.
  • Performance tests and observation: a test of knowledge or skill, written or practical. Tests must be reliable and valid, and can be costly to build.

Don't confuse ranking with rating. Ranking compares people with each other, so someone must come last even in a strong team. Rating compares each person with a scale or standard, so everyone can score high. Judging people against others rather than a standard is the contrast effect, a perception error.

Where it breaks. Most of these methods rate traits, not results, and look back rather than forward. They leave room for personal bias, and several give the employee little to act on. That is why firms added the modern methods.

For exams. Match each description to its name. Remember that the critical incident technique is also a job-analysis tool, and that paired comparison has its own formula.

Rank, pair, scale, tick, incident, secret report.

blocks.title: Modern appraisal methods
blocks.html:
A bank wants to know more than what a branch officer achieved. It wants to know how she treats juniors, and whether she could run a branch. One manager's yearly rating cannot answer both.

In plain wordsModern appraisal methods look at results, behaviour and potential, often through several people's eyes, not just the boss's.

Exam definitionA standard textbook grouping: the modern methods are 360-degree feedback, management by objectives (MBO), behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS), assessment centres, psychological appraisal and human resource accounting.

MethodHow it worksStrengthLimit
360-degree feedbackRatings from supervisor, peers, subordinates, customers and the person themselfA rounded view; good for interpersonal skills and developmentNeeds a mature, trusting culture; multiple raters may be uneven or unkind
Management by objectivesManager and employee set goals together, then compare results with themFocuses on measurable results; suits managersNot for every job; may favour short-term goals
BARSEach point on the scale is described by an example of behaviourMore accurate and fair than trait scalesSlow and costly to build
Assessment centreTrained observers watch people in simulated tasksGood at forecasting future performanceCostly; interpersonal skills can sway ratings
Psychological appraisalTrained psychologists use interviews and testsAssesses potential and personal traitsSlow, costly, depends on the psychologist
Human resource accountingCounts the employee's cost and value in moneyLinks people to financial returnHard to put a fair rupee value on people

360-degree feedback. Anyone with useful information about how a person works can rate them.

Management by objectives (MBO) was set out by Peter Drucker in 1954. The process has four steps:

  1. Set goals and desired results for each subordinate, jointly.
  2. Set performance standards.
  3. Compare actual results with the goals.
  4. Set new goals, and new plans for the goals that were missed.

A sales officer might agree to bring in forty new accounts in the year. At the review, the count of accounts opened, not the manager's impression, decides the rating.

BARS was developed by Smith and Kendall in 1963. Its builders gather examples of effective and ineffective behaviour for a job and place them on the scale as anchors. Here is a customer-handling scale for a bank teller (an illustration):

RatingBehaviour that anchors it
7, excellentLeaves the counter to guide a confused senior citizen through the form
4, averageAnswers the question asked but offers nothing more
1, poorTells a customer to come back tomorrow without checking

The rater picks the description that matches what they saw, which is harder to bend than choosing "good" or "average".

Assessment centres grew out of officer selection in the Second World War. Candidates work through in-basket exercises, group discussions, role plays and simulations, while trained observers score them against set criteria such as planning, decision making and persuasion. They suit promotion to management but cost a lot.

Psychological appraisal aims at future potential. It uses in-depth interviews, psychological tests and talks with supervisors to look at emotional, intellectual and motivational traits.

Human resource accounting sets the cost of recruiting, training and keeping an employee against the value they generate. In textbooks it is also called the cost accounting method of appraisal.

Don't confuse BARS with a graphic rating scale. A graphic scale labels its points with words such as poor, average and good, applied to traits. BARS labels each point with a description of behaviour someone can observe.

Where it breaks. No modern method removes rater bias; BARS still suffers the distortions common to rating, and a 360 can turn into a popularity contest. MBO can push people to hit easy numbers and neglect what is not measured. Many of these methods are also costly, so small firms rarely use them all.

For exams. Match names to ideas: Drucker with MBO, Smith and Kendall with BARS, simulations with assessment centres, "potential" with psychological appraisal.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Your plant adds 360-degree ratings for supervisors and links them to the annual bonus. Ratings from subordinates rise sharply, and several supervisors begin trading favourable marks. Do you keep the pay link or drop it? When pay depends on ratings, raters may inflate or trade marks. Many firms keep 360 for development and use other evidence for pay.

Links. The cross-cultural chapter (this unit) warns that where power distance is high, juniors may rate every boss at the top; anonymity helps. The Johari window in interpersonal behaviour (this unit) explains the value of 360: the blind area is what others see in you and you do not.

360 sources, objectives, behaviour anchors, simulations, psychologists, money.

blocks.title: Rater errors and fair appraisal
blocks.html:
Two supervisors rate the same fitter. One gives him 9 out of 10 on everything, the other 5 out of 10 on everything. Neither looked at his work record. The problem lies in the raters, not in the fitter.

In plain wordsA rater error is a habit of the person rating that pulls the score away from what the employee really did.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: appraisal bias, or rater error, is an inaccurate distortion of measurement, arising from the rater's own judgement rather than the employee's performance.

ErrorWhat happensExample
Halo effectOne strong trait lifts the rating on everythingFew absences, so the rater scores him high on quality too
Horn effectOne weak trait drags down the rating on everythingCasual dress, so "he must be casual about work too"
LeniencyThe rater gives high marks to avoid conflictAll ten staff rated "excellent"
StrictnessThe rater marks harshly, focusing on faultsA manager who thinks no one deserves above average
Central tendencyThe rater puts everyone in the middleEveryone gets 3 out of 5, to play safe
Recency effectThe latest events outweigh the whole periodA mistake last month cancels eleven good months
First impression (primacy)An early impression sticks and colours later ratingsA good first week is never revised
SpilloverPast performance is assumed to continue"He was excellent three years ago, so he must be fine"
Personal bias and stereotypingLiking, background or group beliefs affect the ratingFavouring someone from one's own home town

Leniency and strictness work in opposite directions. Both, with central tendency, make a system useless, because if everyone gets the same rating it tells the firm nothing about who differs.

Don't confuse the halo effect with an appraisal method. The halo effect is a rater error, in which one trait colours the whole judgement. BARS, MBO and 360-degree feedback are methods used to appraise. An exam question that asks which of these is not a method of performance appraisal has the halo effect as its answer. The perception chapter (this unit) covers the halo and horn effects as general perception errors.

Making appraisal fair. No rule removes these errors, but a few habits cut them:

  • Use clear standards drawn from the job description, not general impressions.
  • Rate one dimension for all employees before moving to the next, to weaken the halo.
  • Keep a running record of incidents all year, against recency and first impression.
  • Use more than one rater, or hold a calibration meeting where supervisors compare ratings.
  • Train raters, and let the employee comment on or question the rating.

Why firms bother: benefits and challenges.

GroupBenefitsChallenges
EmployeesClear expectations and goals; recognition; career development; feedback and learningFear of unfair ratings; feedback that feels like punishment
OrganisationBetter productivity; high performers kept; alignment with strategy; evidence for promotion and training decisionsBias and subjectivity; heavy time and cost; managers avoiding hard talks; different standards in different departments

Appraisal also feeds decisions: who is promoted, whose pay rises, who needs training, and who is not meeting standards.

The feedback conversation. A review is only useful if the person leaves knowing what to do. A few rules help:

  • Hold it one to one, and not only once a year; quarterly reviews are a common minimum.
  • Talk about specific results and behaviour, with examples, not about the person's character.
  • Let the employee speak first, and listen.
  • End with agreed actions and a date to check.

Where it breaks. A fair process still cannot make a rating perfect. Rating is a judgement, and a rating tied to pay can make people hide problems. Managers who dread the conversation soften or delay it. That is feedback avoidance, and it is one of the main challenges.

For exams. Expect "name the error" from a short case, and the benefits and challenges as a list.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Head office tells you to use a forced distribution on your team of eight: a few top ratings, most average, a few bottom. All eight met their targets. Forcing a bottom group means rating someone low for the sake of the curve. That can hurt trust and push people to compete rather than help each other. A calibration meeting, which tests ratings against evidence, may serve better than a fixed curve.

Links. Job evaluation (this unit) rates the job, not the person, and appraisal rates the person in the job. Compensation management (this unit) covers the incentive plans that appraisal results often feed.

The rater is the problem: halo, horn, lenient, strict, middle, recent.

chapters.title: Career Planning and Development
chapters.scope: What a career is and how it moves, how careers are planned and developed, how organisations plan for succession, and career paths, plateaus and anchors.

blocks.title: Careers, Schein's cone and career stages
blocks.html:
A bank clerk is promoted to officer. A year later she moves from loans to the treasury desk. Later still, she is asked to join the committee that sets branch targets. All three are career moves, but each is a different kind of move.

In plain wordsA career is the series of jobs and roles a person holds over a working life, with the experience each one adds.

Exam definitionA career is an individually perceived sequence of attitudes and behaviours associated with work-related experiences and activities over the span of a person's life (Douglas T. Hall). Edwin Flippo's version: a sequence of separate but related work activities that gives continuity, order and meaning to a person's life.

Schein's cone. Edgar Schein pictured an organisation as a cone and said a career can move in three directions. Each direction crosses a different kind of boundary.

MovementBoundary crossedWhat changesThe bank clerk
VerticalHierarchicalRank, up (promotion) or down (demotion)Clerk becomes officer
CircumferentialFunctionalFunction or department, at the same levelLoans desk to treasury desk
RadialInclusionCloseness to the centre: more trust, influence and access to decisionsJoins the committee that sets targets

Radial movement needs no promotion. A senior clerk whom the manager consults before every big decision has moved inward, though her title has not changed.

Career stages. A career also moves through time. The standard scheme has five stages. The ages are rough guides.

StageRough ageWhat happens
1 ExplorationUp to about 25The person studies, narrows down the choice of work and forms expectations of it. These are often unrealistic.
2 EstablishmentAbout 25 to 35The first real job. Expectations meet reality. The newcomer learns from a mentor, makes mistakes and earns a place.
3 Mid-careerAbout 35 to 45No longer a beginner, so mistakes are taken seriously. The person asks whether she is advancing, steady or slipping, and balances work with family.
4 Late careerAbout 45 until retirementThe person reaches a level that may be growth or a plateau. Many become mentors to younger staff.
5 DeclineNear and at retirementWork winds down and the person prepares to leave. Letting go can be hard, especially for someone still performing well.

Don't confuse the stage schemes. Textbooks differ on the ages and on how many stages there are. Super's scheme runs growth, exploration, establishment, maintenance and disengagement. Greenhaus's has preparation for work, organisational entry, early career, mid-career and late career, with overlapping ages. Another common list has four: establishment, advancement, maintenance and withdrawal. Learn the five above with their ages as rough guides, and note which scheme your course uses.

Where it breaks. The stages describe a typical working life that runs in one line. Real careers include breaks, a change of field at 40, and returns after years away. A person can be in the exploration stage of a new field at 45. Use the stages to ask what a person needs now, not to decide what they should be doing.

For exams. Know the three directions of the cone and which is which: vertical is rank, circumferential is function, radial is closeness to the centre. Know the five stages in order.

Cone: up and down, across, and inward. Stages: explore, establish, mid, late, decline.

blocks.title: Career planning, management and development
blocks.html:
An engineer at an auto-parts firm in Pune wants to run a plant one day. Her manager sees her as a specialist. Neither has said so. Career planning is how such hopes become visible and get a plan, and these three terms say who does what.

In plain wordsCareer planning is deciding where you want to go in your work and how you will get there.

Exam definitionCareer planning is the process by which a person selects career goals and the path to those goals (Werther and Davis). A fuller textbook version: a deliberate process of becoming aware of oneself, opportunities and constraints, identifying career goals, and programming work, education and experience to reach them.

Three terms sit close together. Werther and Davis set them out like this, and a broader textbook wording follows.

TermUsually the work ofWhat it means
Career planningThe individualChoosing career goals and the path to them
Career developmentThe individual, helped by the organisationThe personal improvements a person makes to carry out the plan. In a broader sense, an ongoing process of moving through career stages
Career managementThe organisation, with the individualDesigning and carrying out goals, plans and strategies so that the organisation meets employees' needs while individuals reach their career goals. In a broader sense, preparing, carrying out and monitoring career plans

The seven steps of career planning. Here they are for Meera, a junior accountant at the same Pune firm. The figures are an illustration.

StepWhat it involvesMeera
1 Self-assessmentStrengths, weaknesses, interests and career valuesGood with numbers, dislikes selling, values a steady job
2 Explore optionsResearch career paths that fit the assessmentCost accounting, internal audit, finance control
3 Set SMART goalsSpecific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-boundBecome assistant cost manager within four years
4 Develop an action planCourses, projects, certificationsA cost-accounting course, and one costing project
5 Acquire required skillsTraining, education, experienceCompletes the course and works with the costing team
6 Seek feedbackRegular feedback, mentorship, improvementReviews progress each quarter with her mentor
7 Monitor and adjustRevise goals as circumstances changeThe firm starts a new product line, so she adds product-costing skills

Why organisations bother. A firm that supports career planning attracts and keeps able people, offers promotions that people can plan for and prepares staff for future challenges. It makes better use of its managerial reserves and places people better. It also cuts dissatisfaction and turnover and lifts morale. Employees gain too. They learn what opportunities exist, pick work that suits their life and family, and tend to commit more when they can see a future.

Tools and initiatives. An organisation supports careers through five usual initiatives: career planning workshops, mentoring, career counselling, coaching and personal development plans (PDPs). A PDP is a written plan of the skills and experience a person will build, with dates, so progress can be tracked. Online learning gives flexible skill-building alongside these.

What the individual can do. Employees also act for themselves. They perform well enough to deserve a chance and make their skills and results known to those who decide on promotions (exposure). They seek guidance, move to another job in the firm, or leave if better options lie elsewhere.

Don't rely on the nesting of the three terms. Some textbooks call career management the umbrella that covers planning and development. Others say career development contains planning and management. Both are common. Learn each term's own definition and say which book you follow.

Where it breaks. A plan can raise hopes that the organisation cannot meet, especially in a flat structure with few promotions. Developed staff are also more employable elsewhere. And a plan built on today's jobs can fail when the business changes.

In practice. The person owns the plan; the organisation supplies information, chances to grow and support. A manager's most useful move is an honest talk about where the person stands.

For exams. Know the seven steps in order, the five initiatives (this list has come up as a question) and Werther and Davis's definitions.

Go deeper for practitioners

Setting up a career development system. A common four-step approach runs as follows. First, assess needs. Second, agree a vision that links those needs to the interventions that meet them. Third, draw up an action plan with top management's support. Fourth, fold the programmes into the firm's training and management development, and evaluate them from time to time. The last step stops career development from becoming a separate, forgotten scheme.

Another seven-step list. Some textbooks give the process in a different form. Analyse the person's skills and abilities. Analyse opportunities inside and outside the firm. Analyse what each career demands. Relate specific jobs to career opportunities. Set realistic short- and long-term goals. Form a strategy for change and adjustment. Prepare and carry out an action plan. It covers the same ground as the list above, starting from analysis instead of self-assessment.

A decision. A high performer tells you she will leave unless she gets a promotion you cannot offer this year. Do you promise one, offer a lateral move with a bigger role, or accept the loss? The honest answer depends on what you can deliver, since a broken promise costs more than an open refusal.

blocks.title: Succession planning
blocks.html:
A plant head retires on 31 March. Nobody has been told who takes over, and the two likeliest candidates have never run a budget. The plant limps through a bad year. Succession planning is how a firm avoids that.

In plain wordsSuccession planning means getting people ready now for important jobs that will fall vacant later.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: succession planning is the systematic process of identifying and developing future leaders to fill an organisation's key positions.

Its aims are leadership continuity, keeping the knowledge senior people hold and being ready for sudden vacancies. It lowers risk and strengthens long-term stability. The successor may come from inside or from outside, but the plan works mainly by building internal candidates. It matters most in an organisation that is growing steadily and has staff who can take on more.

The six steps. They follow a logical order. You cannot map the skills of a job you have not chosen, and you cannot judge readiness before you know what the job needs.

StepAt the Pune plant (an illustration)
1 Identify key positionsPlant head, chief accountant, and the tool-room supervisor, whose skill nobody else has
2 Map competenciesThe plant head needs budgeting, people leadership and knowledge of safety law
3 Identify potential successorsTwo production managers and a quality head are shortlisted
4 Assess readinessAppraisal records and 360-degree feedback show one is ready in a year, one in three
5 Build development plansA budget-owning project, a mentor from head office, a leadership course
6 Implement and monitorReview every year; revise if a successor leaves or the plant changes

Don't confuse succession planning with career planning. Career planning starts with the employee and her goals. Succession planning starts with the organisation's key jobs and asks who can fill them.

BasisCareer planningSuccession planning
FocusEmployeeOrganisation
ObjectiveIndividual career goalsKey positions and future leaders
OutcomeCareer growth and developmentLeadership continuity
Time horizonLong-term, for the individualLong-term, for the organisation
ScopeAll employeesKey and high-potential employees

The two meet in the middle. A person on a succession list needs a career plan that matches it, and a good career plan tells the organisation whom to put on the list.

Links to other chapters. In human resource planning, replacement charts are the simple form of succession planning: for each key post they name likely successors and show how ready each one is. In training and development, the talent pipeline is the flow of people being readied for bigger jobs, and succession planning fills the gap when no one is ready.

Where it breaks. Plans can favour people who resemble today's leaders. Named successors may expect the job as of right, while people not named may lose heart. Plans go stale when the strategy shifts and the key skills change.

For exams. Learn the six steps in the order above. Diagrams of the process sometimes show the steps in a circle without numbers, and a circle can be read starting from the wrong box. Expect the career planning versus succession planning table, as employee-focused against organisation-focused.

Go deeper for practitioners

Readiness. Many firms label each candidate as ready now, ready in a year or two, or needing longer. Many also plot performance against potential on a nine-box grid. A high performer with limited potential is valuable in her present job but not necessarily a successor.

A decision. A family-owned auto-parts firm must choose between the founder's son, who is keen but has run nothing larger than a showroom, and a senior manager who has run the plant for ten years. A development plan with a clear test, such as running a unit with its own targets for two years, lets the family judge on evidence. It also tells the manager what he can expect, so he is less likely to leave.

blocks.title: Career paths, plateau and anchors
blocks.html:
Two clerks join the same bank branch in the same year. One is promoted twice. The other has done the same work for eight years and is told to be patient. Both are on career paths, and the second has reached a plateau.

In plain wordsA career path is the route of jobs a person follows over time, inside one organisation or across several.

Exam definitionA career path is the sequential pattern of jobs that forms a career (Werther and Davis). The term is used interchangeably with career ladder.

A person may move up most of the time, but also sideways or into another function. Textbooks list three kinds of path, according to where the path comes from.

KindWhat it isBasisUse
HistoricalThe paths people have actually followed to get where they areInformal and traditionalPromotions and transfers. It tends to continue how careers have always run
OrganisationalPaths management sets to meet staffing needsOrganisational need and management styleUsually consistent with job evaluation and pay. It reflects management's views of careers
BehaviouralPaths that are logically possible from an analysis of the work done in each jobFormal analysis of the optionsCareer planning. It can open new options and call for change

Career mobility is movement across grades and positions, upward or downward, or a complete change of occupation. Either side can start it: the employee by choice, or the employer by transfer, promotion or demotion. Mobility should be planned, with transition support and training where people change roles, inside or outside the firm.

Career plateau is a point in the career path where the chance of promotion is low and the work becomes repetitive. Hierarchies narrow toward the top, so after some point there are fewer posts above. Two causes are usual. Structurally, no higher post is open (a structural plateau). Or the job no longer teaches the person anything (a content plateau). A plateaued person may still perform well. Ways to respond include a lateral move, job rotation, a bigger role in the same job, a mentoring role or retraining.

Career anchors. Edgar Schein found that people hold on to one theme that they will not give up when they must choose. He called it the career anchor: a person's self-image of their talents, motives and values, formed through real work experience. Schein's early research found five anchors, and later work extended the list to eight.

AnchorWhat the person will not give up
Technical or functional competenceBecoming excellent at a craft or specialism
General managerial competenceResponsibility for people and results
Autonomy or independenceWorking by one's own rules and schedule
Security or stabilityA steady job and a predictable future
Entrepreneurial creativityBuilding something of one's own
Service or dedication to a causeWork that serves values the person cares about
Pure challengeSolving hard problems and beating tough opponents
LifestyleA balance of work, family and personal life

An anchor is found by self-assessment. Someone anchored in security fits a public-sector bank. Someone anchored in autonomy may prefer consulting or freelance work.

Don't confuse a plateau with the decline stage, or an anchor with a goal. A plateau can come at 35 and the decline stage comes near retirement. A goal is a future position; an anchor is the underlying value that makes some positions satisfying and others not.

Where it breaks. Career paths drawn from history copy the past, including its bias. An anchor rests on self-report, can shift with life events and tends to show only after some years of real work. Treat a result as a start for discussion, not a verdict.

In practice. Matching assignments to a person's anchor helps. Offering an expert a ladder that rewards skill, without forcing a move into management, keeps people who are anchored in technical competence.

For exams. Know the three path types, the definition of mobility and plateau, and that the anchor concept is Schein's.

chapters.title: Talent Management and Skill Development
chapters.scope: How organisations manage the whole path of capable people, through five phases, three strategies and a seven-step framework, and how skill gaps are found and closed through soft, functional and management skills.

blocks.title: What talent management is
blocks.html:
Suppose a Pune auto-parts plant loses its senior maintenance engineer to a rival. HR learns of it from the resignation letter. Nobody was being prepared as a successor, and the post stays empty for months. The plant had hired, trained and appraised its people, yet nobody was looking after the path of its key people as a whole.

In plain wordsTalent management means looking after capable people as one connected path: finding them, hiring them, growing them, keeping them and preparing their replacements.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: talent management is the full scope of HR processes to attract, onboard, develop, motivate and retain high-performing employees. A common longer wording calls it a continuous process of identifying, attracting, nurturing and retaining people whose skills, values and aspirations match the organisation's goals.

Its aim is a high-performance workforce that drives innovation, adapts to challenges and supports the organisation's mission. It joins HR activities that are often run separately. It starts before hiring, with a forecast of need, and it goes on past a person's last day, through the knowledge they leave behind.

The seven processes it ties together.

ProcessWhat it does
Workforce planningMaps the talent the organisation will need in future
Recruitment and onboardingAttracts capable people and brings them into the culture
Performance managementSets goals, assesses results and improves them
Learning and developmentGives continuous learning and growth
Employee engagementBuilds purpose, connection and recognition
Succession planningPrepares future leaders
RetentionKeeps people through career paths, rewards and a positive experience of work

Three of these have chapters in this unit: Human Resource Planning (workforce planning), Recruitment and Selection, and Training and Development. Performance Management and Appraisal covers how results are set and judged. Career Planning and Development covers career paths and succession.

Why it matters to the business. Each benefit below is a claim about what happens when the processes work together. It is not a guarantee.

BenefitHow it comes about
Business performancePeople with the right skills are matched to the strategic goals
Competitive advantageA skilled, future-ready workforce is hard for rivals to copy
InnovationTrusted, well-developed people are more willing to try new ideas and take risks
Productive teamsTrust, collaboration and accountability build up over time
Lower turnoverFeedback, recognition and autonomy lift morale, so fewer people leave
Employer brandingA name for growing people attracts better applicants
Growth and developmentInternal capability reduces the need to hire from outside

Don't confuse talent management with HRM, or with succession planning. HRM covers everything about people at work, including pay administration and industrial relations. Talent management follows the flow of capable people. Succession planning is one process inside it. Strategic HRM (this unit) aligns all HR activity with strategy; talent management applies that alignment to the workforce's capability.

Where it breaks. Firms use the word "talent" in two ways. Some mean a small group of high performers; others mean every employee. Investing only in a chosen few can discourage everyone else. Critics also say talent management is old HR practice under a new name. It earns its place only when the processes are joined up and tied to strategy. And its benefits are hard to prove: turnover can fall for many reasons.

In practice. Take any key post and ask who could fill it if the holder left tomorrow, and who in a year. If the answer is nobody, talent management is missing, whatever the HR calendar says.

For exams. Learn the seven processes and the wording "holistic, integrated, goal-oriented process of planning, recruiting, selecting, developing, managing and compensating employees". A past question gave that wording and asked for the term. The answer is talent management, since it spans the whole path, where HR planning covers only the forecast.

Attract, develop, motivate, retain: the whole path of capable people.

blocks.title: The five phases and three strategies
blocks.html:
Suppose a chain of diagnostic labs in Hyderabad hires well, yet every few months an experienced technician leaves and the know-how leaves with her. More hiring does not fix that. Talent management works in five phases, and each phase sets up the next.

PhaseWhat it doesTypical methods
1 PlanningTies the talent plan to the organisation's goals; forecasts the talent it will need; bridges capability gapsPredictive analytics, workforce forecasts
2 AttractingFinds people for more than the vacancy of the day, including those not looking for a jobEmployer branding, social media, referrals
3 DevelopingGrows people for future roles by widening their skills and knowledgeMentoring, shadowing, rotational programmes, learning experience platforms
4 RetainingKeeps people longer by strengthening their commitmentInclusion, belonging, wellness, flexibility
5 TransitioningPlans moves and exits so that knowledge stays in the organisationInternal mobility, cross-functional projects, leadership grooming, mentoring, documentation

A passive candidate is someone who has a job and is not searching, but might move for a good offer. A learning experience platform is an online system that recommends learning content to each person. Both are examples of methods, not requirements. Knowledge management, the aim of phase 5, means capturing and sharing what people know, so that it stays when they move on.

Three strategies for finding talent. Phase 2 and phase 3 raise a choice: buy ready talent, grow it, or do both.

StrategyStrengthsCosts and risks
Hire elite talentExpertise arrives at once; sets a high-performance benchmark; faster growth; readier for challenges and risksCostly; may unsettle insiders who were passed over
Nurture emerging talentFaster to find; cheaper per head; builds loyal people aligned with the organisation's valuesSlower to deliver; development costs time and money; trained people may leave
Blend bothExperience plus fresh energy; elite hires mentor and pass on knowledge, and emerging talent grows fasterNeeds managers who will mentor, and fair handling of pay gaps

The costs column is reasoning, not research findings.

An illustration, not market data. A firm can pay ₹30 lakh a year for one proven manager, or ₹12 lakh each for two promising specialists. Two cost 2 × ₹12 lakh = ₹24 lakh, and the firm has two people to grow. The price is time: the specialists take longer to reach the proven manager's level.

Don't confuse the five phases with the seven processes. The phases are stages of the talent cycle. The processes (in the last block) are the HR functions that carry the stages out: recruitment and onboarding sit mainly in attracting, and succession planning in transitioning. Some lists start with "identify" in place of planning; the ground covered is the same.

Where it breaks. The cycle is tidier than life. Retention starts on a person's first day, not in phase 4, and transitioning must handle sudden exits as well as planned ones. No strategy wins everywhere: critical posts that need proven skill lean to hiring elite talent, and large volumes of entry roles lean to nurturing.

For exams. Know the five phases in order and one strength of each strategy. Elite hiring gives speed, nurturing gives loyalty and lower cost, and the blend gives mentoring and knowledge transfer.

Plan, attract, develop, retain, transition.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Your plant must fill a lead-engineer post within eight weeks. An insider is about 70% ready and would grow into it with a mentor. An outside expert is fully ready but asks for much more pay, and the insider has hinted she would leave if passed over. Hiring the expert buys speed and risks losing a loyal person; promoting the insider saves money and risks a shaky first year.

A blend may be possible: promote the insider, hire a senior consultant for six months to mentor her, and write down what the consultant teaches. Ask how costly an error in the post would be, and how long the gap can last. The answer to those two questions usually settles the choice.

blocks.title: The seven-step framework
blocks.html:
Suppose a hospital opens a new wing and hires forty nurses in a month. Nobody plans their first week, their learning or their way up, and many leave within the year. The seven-step framework is a checklist that covers the whole path, from knowing the skills you need to preparing the next leaders.

In plain wordsThe framework is a seven-part checklist for running talent management as one continuous process.

Exam formThe seven steps: specify the skills needed; attract the right people; onboard and organise work; organise learning and development; hold performance appraisals; strategise to retain your best talent; plan for succession.

StepWhat to doExample tools
1 Specify skillsTurn the business strategy into the skills required. First ask whether existing staff can be taught the skill; if so, there is no need to hireBusiness strategy mapped to the skills it requires
2 AttractRun targeted job advertisements on the right sites, supported by employer branding. Interview, and add personality assessments, references and tests of real work. Then hireGamified applications, video job previews, virtual job fairs
3 OnboardBe ready before the person arrives: know the tasks, schedule the training and assign a colleague to helpInteractive portals, real-time feedback
4 Learn and developPlan courses, conferences and a learning management system. Developing current staff is often easier than hiring, and even top hires want to learnTraditional training plus AI-based personalised learning
5 AppraiseCheck performance regularly. It shows who can take on more, which can save an outside hire and prepare someone for promotion360-degree feedback, pulse surveys, real-time dashboards
6 RetainKeep people satisfied: promotions, benefits, motivation, job satisfaction and a better cultureRegular check-ins, job crafting, internal gig platforms
7 Plan successionPrepare people for senior posts, such as when a senior member retires, through continuous learning and knowledge managementLeadership labs, innovation incubators

The tools in the last column are examples that some firms use, not requirements. A firm that uses plain interviews, classroom training and a yearly appraisal still follows the framework. A 360-degree appraisal gathers views from a person's manager, peers and reports. A pulse survey is a short questionnaire repeated often. In job crafting, employees reshape parts of their own tasks or working relationships. An internal gig platform lists short projects that any employee can take on.

Why the order matters. Step 1 comes first because advertising before the need is clear brings in the wrong people. Step 5 feeds step 4 and step 7, because appraisal shows who is ready for more. Steps 1, 2 and 4 draw on Human Resource Planning, Recruitment and Selection and Training and Development in this unit.

Don't confuse the seven steps with the seven processes. They overlap heavily, and both lists have seven items. The processes name the HR functions, such as engagement and retention. The steps put the functions in an order of use, starting from the skills needed.

Where it breaks. Real firms do not move through the steps once. Appraisal runs all year, and retention work starts at onboarding. A small firm cannot run seven formal programmes. New tools cost money, and a pulse survey is wasted if nobody acts on the answers. No tool improves hiring unless it measures what the job needs.

In practice. A small firm can start with two questions. Which skills will we need next year? Who is ready to take over our key jobs? Those two questions are steps 1 and 7, and the other steps follow from them.

For exams. Know the seven steps in order, the first step (specify the skills needed), and that step 7 involves knowledge management.

Skills, attract, onboard, learn, appraise, retain, succeed.

blocks.title: Skill development and its three pillars
blocks.html:
A plant's best machine operator becomes a shift supervisor. He knows every machine, but he avoids giving feedback and cannot explain a cost problem to the manager. His skills no longer match his job. Skill development is how the gap is found and closed.

In plain wordsSkill development means finding out which skills you lack for the work, then building them with practice and learning.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: skill development is the intentional effort to enhance an individual's ability to perform, adapt and evolve through targeted learning. It has two parts: identifying skill gaps, then developing and honing the skills. Its strategic value lies in innovation, organisational agility, job satisfaction and role mastery.

A skill is the ability to do something well. People carry out their plans only as well as their skills allow, so a gap in skills becomes a gap in results. Skill development is where talent management meets the learning process described in Training and Development.

The three pillars.

PillarFocusExamples
Soft skills (behavioural)Emotional intelligence, cultural sensitivity, decision-making. They matter most in client handling, leadership and influencing othersConflict resolution, negotiation, empathy, storytelling, resilience; also teamwork, communication, time management
Functional skills (technical)The technical knowledge needed to run operations and solve problems in real situationsBudgeting, spreadsheet modelling, digital literacy, technical writing
Management skills (Katz's triad)The abilities a manager needs: conceptual, human and technicalBusiness model design, restructuring (conceptual); coaching, conflict mediation (human); coding, CAD design, lab experiments (technical)

Soft skills are wanted in almost every profession. "Soft" contrasts them with the "hard" skills of a trade. In Katz's triad, conceptual skill is working with abstract ideas and seeing the organisation whole, human skill is working with and through people, and technical skill is the skill the job itself needs. Principles of Management (Unit 1) shows which level of manager needs which, so it is not repeated here.

A skill gap, worked out. An illustration: the new supervisor is rated on a 1 to 5 scale against what the new job needs.

Skill (Katz)NeededHas nowGap
Technical35None (surplus of 2)
Human424 − 2 = 2
Conceptual323 − 2 = 1

The largest gap is in human skill, which is a soft skill, so the plan starts there: coaching, practice in giving feedback and a mentor. The smaller conceptual gap can be closed later through a cross-department project.

Don't confuse the pillars with each other. "Functional skills" is used in three senses. Here it means job-related technical ability. It also means skills that transfer between jobs, and, in some countries' vocational schemes, basic English, mathematics and computer skills. Check which sense a question uses. The pillars also overlap: Katz's human skill is much like soft skill, and Katz's technical skill is much like functional skill.

Where it breaks. The boundaries are blurry. Negotiation is a soft skill, yet it also needs conceptual judgement. Calling skills "soft" can make them seem optional, although many promotions turn on them. And a single course seldom builds a skill; practice with feedback does.

In practice. Compare what the role needs with what the person has, then match the method to the pillar: practice and coaching for soft skills, courses and on-the-job practice for functional skills, and rotation and projects for managerial skills.

For exams. Know the two parts of skill development, the three pillars with an example of each, and Katz's three skills. Technical skill is also called hard skill.

Find the gap, then build the skill: soft, functional, managerial.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Your team lead has the largest gap in conceptual skill, and the only affordable programme is a two-week classroom course on strategy. A six-month cross-department project would build the skill better but removes her from daily work. Which cost is higher, a thin course or a thin team for six months?

One way through is a shorter project stretch, with a mentor who reviews her thinking each month. The deciding facts are how soon the firm needs the skill and how much she can safely leave behind.

chapters.title: Employee Engagement and Work-Life Balance
chapters.scope: What employee engagement is (Kahn's dimensions, levels, Gallup's typology), how to build and measure it, and work-life balance: principles, strategies, benefits, warning signs, burnout and what employers can do.

blocks.title: What employee engagement is
blocks.html:
Two agents in a call centre have the same pay, the same shift and the same manager. One stays on the line until the customer's problem is solved and suggests a change to the script. The other follows the checklist, then logs off on the dot. Employee engagement is the name for that difference.

In plain wordsEngagement is how much of themselves people put into their work: energy, attention and care, beyond the minimum the job asks.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: employee engagement is the level of enthusiasm and dedication a person feels toward the job. William Kahn (1990) described it as people bringing and expressing themselves physically, cognitively and emotionally in their work roles.

Why it matters. Engaged employees tend to show five things:

  • higher productivity, with effort beyond the job description;
  • longer stay, so lower hiring and training costs;
  • better service, which raises customer satisfaction and loyalty;
  • lower absenteeism;
  • better health and fewer workplace injuries.

Most of this evidence comes from surveys, which show that engagement and good results move together. They do not prove that engagement causes the results.

Kahn's three dimensions. Kahn said people engage in three ways at once. Think of the agent who stays on the line.

DimensionWhat the person bringsWhat it looks likeThe agent who stays
PhysicalEnergy and effortAttentive, punctual, willing to take on hard tasksStays on the line past the target time
CognitiveAttention and thinkingFocus, problem-solving, new ideasWorks out why the script fails and suggests a fix
EmotionalCare, pride and trustBelonging, persistence, speaking well of the organisationWants this customer to be treated well

Levels of engagement. Organisations often sort staff into four levels. Each level needs a different response.

LevelHow people behaveWhat helps
Highly engagedEnthusiastic, take initiative, help others; speak well of the employerUse them as role models and mentors
Moderately engagedPerform well, like the organisation, but see things to improve and invest less emotionallyFind what holds them back; they can become high performers
Barely engagedIndifferent; do just enough; may be looking elsewhereAct early; they are a turnover risk
DisengagedNegative about the employer; cut off from its goals; may resist change and harm team moraleIntervene quickly, before the mood spreads

Gallup's typology uses three groups. Engaged employees are enthusiastic and committed, and they bring ideas. Not engaged employees put in time but not energy or passion, and wait to be told what to do. Actively disengaged employees are unhappy and show it, working against colleagues' efforts and lowering morale.

Don't confuse engagement with satisfaction or commitment. Satisfaction is a feeling about the job. Organisational commitment is attachment to the employer. Engagement is the energy and attention a person actually brings to the work. Someone can be satisfied but coasting, or committed to the firm but bored. Job satisfaction and commitment are covered in the chapter on personality, perception and attitude.

Don't confuse the lists. Some textbooks describe engagement as emotional, cognitive and behavioural commitment. That is a different list; Kahn's three are physical, cognitive and emotional. Likewise, the four levels above are a common teaching scheme, while Gallup has three groups. Roughly, "not engaged" covers the moderate and barely engaged, and "actively disengaged" matches the disengaged.

Where it breaks. Definitions differ between surveys, so scores from different firms are hard to compare. A keen employee with no authority, tools or time cannot show engagement. And engagement can slide into overwork, which the last two blocks of this chapter take up.

For exams. Know Kahn's three dimensions with an example of each, the four levels, and Gallup's three groups. Questions often ask which dimension an example shows, or what separates "not engaged" from "actively disengaged".

Go deeper for practitioners

Kahn's three conditions. Kahn asked when people bring themselves into a role. He found three psychological conditions. Meaningfulness is a sense of getting a return on the effort. Safety is being able to show oneself without fear of harm to image, status or career. Availability is having the physical, emotional and mental resources to invest. A manager who punishes mistakes removes safety. A heavy overload removes availability.

Work engagement. Wilmar Schaufeli and colleagues (2002) defined work engagement as a positive, fulfilling state of mind marked by vigour, dedication and absorption. It is measured with the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale. It is a state of energy at work, not a trait of the person.

A decision. Your team's survey shows high satisfaction and low engagement: people like the place but do little beyond the task. Do you add perks, or look at the work itself (autonomy, purpose, feedback)? Perks lift satisfaction; the work is what draws energy.

Physical is energy, cognitive is thinking, emotional is attachment.

blocks.title: Building and measuring engagement
blocks.html:
A company runs an annual survey, scores 62% favourable, files the report, and changes nothing. Next year fewer people answer. Building engagement is a cycle meant to stop exactly that: every survey must end in visible action.

In plain wordsBuilding engagement means asking people what drives and drains their energy, then fixing what they name, then checking that it worked.

Exam definitionThe standard five-step process: diagnose and design, survey, analyse, act (action planning), and follow up.

StepWhat happensWhat goes wrong
1 Diagnose and designFind the organisation's needs and priorities, using feedback sessions; tailor the plan to different rolesOne plan copied from another firm
2 SurveyAsk about trust, communication, autonomy, career development and culture; paper or online, whichever staff are comfortable with; keep answers anonymousStaff fear that answers can be traced
3 AnalyseThe most important step. Find what drives people's best work and what pushes them away; present the findingsReporting one average and missing differences between teams
4 ActTurn findings into a few actions (mentoring, training, flexible policies); coach line managers and HR; give each action an owner and a measurable targetToo many actions, and managers not trained to carry them out
5 Follow upCheck whether the actions worked; report back through town halls or newslettersSilence after the survey, which teaches staff not to answer

Measuring engagement. Two numbers are common. An engagement score summarises answers across the survey, usually as an average or a share of favourable answers. There is no single formula, so compare a team with its own past score. The employee Net Promoter Score (eNPS) uses one question: "How likely are you to recommend this organisation as a place to work?", answered from 0 to 10.

  • Promoters answer 9 or 10, passives 7 or 8, detractors 0 to 6.
  • eNPS = % promoters − % detractors. It runs from −100 to +100.
  • Example: of 100 replies, 40 are promoters, 35 passives and 25 detractors. eNPS = 40 − 25 = +15.

Firms also watch turnover, absenteeism and survey response rates.

Drivers of engagement. Surveys differ, but the same drivers keep appearing:

  • Meaningful work and a clear link to the organisation's goals;
  • a supportive manager and trust in leaders;
  • recognition of effort, and fair pay and treatment;
  • growth: learning, a career path, new challenges;
  • voice: two-way communication and a say in decisions;
  • autonomy and a manageable workload, with flexibility and wellbeing support.

These echo ideas from other chapters. Herzberg's motivators (recognition, the work itself, growth) are drivers. In the job demands–resources model, resources such as support, control and feedback drive engagement. Fair treatment and a strong culture matter too.

Don't confuse the engagement score with eNPS. The score says how favourable staff are across many topics. eNPS says how willing they are to recommend the employer, from one question. Neither says why. The comments and the driver questions do.

Where it breaks. Surveys are a snapshot, and small teams can lose anonymity when results are split finely. Frequent surveys tire people. Pushing managers to raise scores can lead them to coach their staff on how to answer. And a driver that matters in one firm may not in another.

In practice. Choose two or three actions, name an owner for each, tell staff what you chose and why, and report progress. A small visible change builds more trust than a large plan nobody sees.

Go deeper for practitioners
