A decision. A depot's eNPS is −10. Comments mention late shift lists and managers who never say thank you. Do you launch a company-wide perks programme, or fix the shift lists first? Fixing what people named, at once, proves the survey was worth answering. Perks answer a question nobody asked.

Why analysis comes before action. Averages hide spread. A score of 60% could mean every team is at 60%, or one team at 95% and another at 25%. Split results by team, role and tenure before choosing actions.

Diagnose, survey, analyse, act, follow up.

blocks.title: Work-life balance and how to build it
blocks.html:
A software engineer in Pune takes client calls at 10 pm and checks mail over dinner. Last month she missed her daughter's school event, and she is now short with her team. Work-life balance asks whether the demands of work and of the rest of life can both be met.

In plain wordsBalance means work and the rest of life each get the time and energy they need, in a mix that suits the person.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: work–life balance describes the relationship between work and the other commitments in a person's life, and how they affect each other.

The rest of life includes family, health, friends, learning, rest and community. Balance helps employees keep both a career and a life, and it helps employers keep motivated, loyal people.

Four principles. The same four ideas appear in most advice on balance:

  • Prioritise what matters most, such as family, health and rest.
  • Reduce stress through exercise, breathing, yoga or counselling.
  • Manage time with clear goals and time blocking.
  • Set boundaries, including saying no when a request cannot be met.

Five practical strategies. The engineer could use each one:

StrategyWhat to doThe engineer
Make a work–leisure planSchedule work, exercise and hobbies in the same diary; switch off work notifications outside work hours; a compressed work week is one optionAgrees when she is reachable and mutes mail after that
Cut what wastes time and energyDrop tasks that help neither work nor leisure; avoid constant multitasking; work in focused blocksStops attending meetings that need only a summary
Delegate or outsourceHand time-consuming tasks to others, matched to their strengths; this also develops themLets a junior run the routine test reports
Schedule restTake annual leave; keep no-meeting days and screen-free weekendsBlocks Sunday evenings for family
Prioritise smartlyRank tasks by urgency and importance; plan early to avoid last-minute rushes; manage client expectationsTells the client when she will reply

A compressed week. Five 8-hour days become four 10-hour days. The total is still 40 hours (4 × 10 = 5 × 8), but the team gains one full free day. The cost is longer, more tiring days.

Benefits. Good balance tends to bring:

  • health: less stress, better sleep, a healthier lifestyle;
  • output: better focus, fewer errors, sharper problem-solving from a rested person;
  • relationships: more time and emotional energy for family and friends;
  • motivation: people who feel their life is working are more attached to the job.

Don't confuse balance with an equal split. A balanced week is not 50% work and 50% life. Balance is what lets a person meet the demands they care about, and it changes with life stage: a new parent and a young graduate need different mixes. It is also not a perk from the employer. Individuals can do much, but the employer sets the job's demands, as the next block shows.

Where it breaks. Personal strategies need a job that allows them. A person with no say over the roster cannot "prioritise smartly". Time-saving advice also assumes the money and help to outsource, which not everyone has. Much of the evidence on benefits is correlational: balanced people may be healthier for other reasons too.

For exams. Know the four principles, the five strategies and the benefits. Questions often ask which strategy fits a case, for example delegating to free time, or muting notifications as a boundary.

Prioritise, reduce stress, manage time, set boundaries.

blocks.title: Imbalance, burnout and the employer's part
blocks.html:
A bank's regional office finds that its best-performing branch also has the most sick leave and two recent resignations. Long hours pay off for a while. Then they start to cost more than they bring.

In plain wordsWork-life imbalance is when work takes so much time and energy that health or the rest of life begins to suffer.

Exam definitionBurnout, the extreme result, is defined by the World Health Organization (ICD-11) as a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It has three features: exhaustion, growing mental distance or cynicism toward the job, and reduced effectiveness.

Imbalance usually grows when the boundary between work and personal life is blurred and not kept up. The signs fall into four groups.

KindSigns
PhysicalExhaustion, frequent illness, headaches, body pain
EmotionalIrritability, mood swings, anxiety, loss of interest and motivation
BehaviouralAbsenteeism, procrastination, projects left unfinished, withdrawal from friends, missing family events
At workMore mistakes, missed deadlines, poorer concentration

Common causes are unrealistic expectations, little control over one's schedule, constant connection to screens and messages, and work that clashes with personal values. Persistent low mood or anxiety needs professional help. This list is not a diagnosis.

The cost to the employer. Imbalance raises absenteeism and turnover and lowers quality, so the cost shows up in the firm's accounts. At the bank branch, two resignations mean two hiring and training bills, plus the work left undone while the posts are empty.

What an employer can do. Primary measures change the work. Secondary ones help people cope.

ActionWhat it looks like
Flexible hours and placeFlexible start times, hybrid or remote work where the job allows, a compressed week
Leave that people actually takeAnnual, parental and sick leave, and sabbaticals; managers who take their own
No-meeting daysOne or two days a week kept clear for focused work
Clear boundariesAgreed hours, no non-urgent messages after hours, no expectation of instant replies
Realistic workloadTargets and staffing that fit the hours; overload is often the root cause
SupportCounselling, wellness programmes, childcare or care-leave help

Back at the branch, the region could reset targets to the staffing level, and require that no non-urgent message goes out after 7 pm. A yoga session on its own would treat the signs and leave the cause.

Don't confuse stress with burnout. Stress is the reaction to demands, and rest and fewer demands can relieve it. Burnout follows when stress goes on for long and is not dealt with. It brings exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of being ineffective. The chapter on emotions and stress covers stress and how to manage it.

Where it breaks. A flexible-hours policy fails if promotions go to the people who answer messages at midnight. Staff read the culture, not the policy. Flexibility can also blur boundaries, as people who work from home sometimes never stop. And some roles, such as emergency services, cannot offer flexible hours.

In practice. Measure the signs: overtime, unused leave, sick days and resignations by team. A team with the longest hours and the most unused leave needs attention before its next resignation.

Go deeper for practitioners

Two paths in the job demands–resources model. High demands with few resources wear people down, which leads toward exhaustion and burnout. Resources such as support, control and feedback lead toward engagement. The same long hours can therefore produce either, depending on what the job gives back. This is why engagement and balance are managed together.

Work–family conflict. Jeffrey Greenhaus and Nicholas Beutell (1985) described three forms. In time-based conflict, hours spent on one role cannot be spent on the other. In strain-based conflict, tiredness or tension from one role spills into the other. In behaviour-based conflict, behaviour suited to one role, such as a commanding style, does not suit the other.

A decision. A top salesperson is hitting targets and working every weekend. Do you praise the results or ask about the weekends? Praise without a question rewards the habit that may end in resignation.

Change the work first; help people cope second.

chapters.title: Organisation Development and Change
chapters.scope: What organisational change is and why people resist it, what organisation development is and how its process runs, the main OD interventions and tools, and Lewin's three-stage model with the benefits and challenges of OD.

blocks.title: Organisational change and resistance
blocks.html:
A public-sector bank branch is told that from next month every transaction will run on a new core-banking system. Some staff are keen, some are afraid, and customers still arrive on Monday. How a change is classified, caused and handled decides how smoothly it goes.

In plain wordsOrganisational change is any real alteration in how an organisation is built, how it works or what it is aiming for.

Exam definitionOrganisational change is any modification in an organisation's structure, processes, culture or strategy. It may be planned or unplanned, and it is necessary for survival and adaptation.

Planned change is deliberate: managers see a need, design a response and manage it. The move to new banking software is planned. Unplanned change is forced by events nobody scheduled, such as a flood that closes the branch and sends staff to a temporary office. Planned change is proactive; unplanned change is reactive.

Change is sorted into four types by what it alters.

TypeWhat it changesExample (an illustration)
StructuralHierarchy, roles, responsibilities and reporting linesA college merges two departments under one head, or moves from functional units to teams
TechnologicalTools, software, automation and digital processesThe branch moves to the new core-banking system
People-orientedAttitudes, behaviour and relationshipsClerks are trained in emotional intelligence and conflict handling for dealing with angry customers
StrategicMission, vision, long-term goals and business directionA regional cooperative bank decides to grow through digital services instead of new branches

Changes rarely arrive alone. The new software is technological, but it also moves tasks between desks (structural) and asks clerks to work differently (people-oriented).

Forces for change come from inside or outside the organisation.

Internal forcesExternal forces
Vision and values, such as a commitment to diversityCompetition from rivals
Culture: a creative culture accepts change more easilyNew technology
Leadership: a new head brings new strategy and styleGovernment rules, taxes and labour law
Unsatisfactory performance, often the sharpest triggerEconomy and politics
Employees' skills and attitudesSocial change: education, urbanisation, migration, tastes
Core expertise, which can open new productsNew market opportunities

Resistance to change is opposition to a change, open or quiet. It shows up as arguing, delay, absence, or workarounds such as keeping a paper register beside the new system.

  • Individual sources: habit; fear of the unknown; fear of losing pay, status or the value of one's skills; hearing only what fits existing views.
  • Organisational sources: rules built to keep things stable; group norms; a threat to the power or expertise of some people; changing one part while the rest stays as before.

John Kotter and Leonard Schlesinger (1979) listed six ways to deal with it. Each suits a different situation.

ApproachUse whenDrawback
Education and communicationPeople lack information or the reasonsSlow when many are involved
Participation and involvementManagers lack some facts and others can resistSlow, and may produce a poor plan
Facilitation and supportPeople struggle to adjust: training, counselling, timeSlow and costly
Negotiation and agreementSomeone loses out and has the power to resistCan be costly, and invites others to bargain
Manipulation and co-optationOther methods fail or cost too muchPeople who feel tricked stop trusting
Explicit and implicit coercionSpeed is vital and managers hold the powerRisky: leaves resentment

Don't confuse the type of change with its cause. The type says what changes: structure, technology, people or strategy. The force says why: competition, a new leader, a new rule. One force, such as a rival's app, can drive changes of all four types.

Where it breaks. The four types are a sorting aid. Real changes cross the lines, and the line between structural and technological is often blurred. Resistance is not always a fault: staff who say the new screen is slower for a common task may be right. Listen before deciding the objection is only fear.

In practice. Ask who gains and who loses before launching. Staff who lose status or skills resist hardest, and the answer shows which approach fits. The last two approaches buy compliance, not commitment, so keep them for real emergencies. Strategic HRM notes that people-focused change meets less resistance; the approaches above show how.

For exams. Know the four types with an example each, the internal and external forces, the sources of resistance, and the six approaches. Older questions also ask for the order of steps in a change effort; the next concept gives it.

Go deeper for practitioners

Leavitt's diamond (1965) treats an organisation as four linked variables: task, structure, technology and people. Change one and the others must adjust. That is why a software-only project so often stalls: the task has changed, but roles, skills and habits have not.

A decision. The branch head has two months. Education, with a clear explanation of why, is cheap but slow. Facilitation, with training and a help desk, costs money and time. Which gap is bigger in her branch: not knowing why, or not knowing how?

What changes: structure, technology, people, strategy. How to win people over: tell, involve, support, bargain, steer, force.

blocks.title: Organisation development and its process
blocks.html:
A college merges its commerce and management departments. A circular announces one head and one timetable. Within a month the staff form two rival camps and each blames the other for clashes. OD starts from the idea that orders alone do not fix this: first find out what is really wrong, with the people concerned.

In plain wordsOrganisation development (OD) is a planned, long-term effort, using facts and the people's own involvement, to make an organisation work better and cope with change.

Exam definitionOD is a planned, systematic, data-driven process aimed at improving an organisation's effectiveness, adaptability and overall health. Richard Beckhard (1969) described it as an effort that is planned, organisation-wide and managed from the top, using behavioural-science knowledge in planned interventions in the organisation's processes.

OD works on people, processes, structure and culture together. It has a human side (culture, behaviour, communication) and a technical side (structure, goals, processes). Work that treats only one side usually fails. In the college, a new timetable is technical; the rivalry between the camps is human.

Objectives. Continuous improvement (including less waste). Employee engagement (participation, upskilling, satisfaction and retention). Organisational learning (shared knowledge and learning from mistakes). Systemic change (policies, hierarchies and team dynamics together).

Characteristics. OD is planned: intentional, research-based, often led by an OD consultant (a change agent, inside or outside). It is collaborative: top management supports it and staff take part, in trust and openness. It is data-driven: surveys, interviews and metrics guide decisions. It uses feedback and reinforcement: change, reinforce, review, adjust.

The OD process has five steps. The right-hand column shows the merged college as an illustration.

StepWhat happensThe college
1 DiagnosisAssess the current state and find the root issues (SWOT, surveys, interviews)Interviews and a student survey show two timetable systems, duplicate subjects and fear for posts
2 Planning interventionsDesign strategies aimed at the root issuesA joint committee for one timetable; a workshop on roles
3 ImplementationRoll out through training, communication and staff involvementWorkshops run; the common timetable starts
4 EvaluationCheck results against objectives (KPIs, follow-up surveys, before-and-after comparison)A second survey after one semester; clashes are counted
5 ReinforcementAdjust, then build what works into policy and cultureWorkload policy revised; the joint committee made permanent

Order of an organisational change effort. Exams ask for this sequence: information gathering, diagnosis, feedback and discussion with the people concerned, planning (a work proposal), implementation, evaluation. Information gathering comes before diagnosis, since facts must exist before anyone can diagnose. Textbooks differ on whether discussion comes before or after the written work proposal, so do not rely on those two alone.

Action research is the classic form of this cycle. Kurt Lewin coined the term in the 1940s: research whose findings go straight into action, and whose results are then studied in turn.

Don't confuse OD with organisational change. Change is any modification, planned or not. OD is one planned, research-based way of managing change, aimed at the organisation's health. Also, books give the OD cycle as four, five or seven steps. Some split planning into design and development; some use diagnosis, action planning, intervention, evaluation. These are the same cycle in more or less detail.

Where it breaks. Real work is not so tidy. Steps overlap, and diagnosis continues during action. OD needs committed top management and takes a long time. Its gains are hard to measure, since many things change at once. Its stress on openness and participation may sit uneasily in a strongly hierarchical culture.

In practice. Diagnose before choosing a remedy. A common failure is to run a favourite training day first and discover afterwards that the problem was structure or trust.

For exams. Know the dual approach, four objectives, four characteristics, the five steps and the seven steps of action research.

Go deeper for practitioners

The McKinsey 7-S framework is a diagnostic checklist, not a sequence. Shared values sit at the centre. Three hard elements surround them: strategy, structure and systems. Three soft elements complete it: style (how top managers lead), skills and staff. Its lesson is that changing one S alone seldom holds. A new structure for the college (hard) will not last if the old rivalry in style and staff (soft) is untouched.

Culture and climate, which diagnosis examines, are covered in the chapter on organisational culture and climate.

A decision. A diagnosis shows both camps agree on strategy but distrust each other's style. Which comes first: redesigning the structure again, or a team-level intervention?

Diagnose, plan, implement, evaluate, reinforce. Information first, action later.

blocks.title: OD interventions and tools
blocks.html:
Diagnosis at the merged college shows two things. The two groups of lecturers hardly talk, and admission papers pass through six desks. One problem concerns people, the other a process, and they need different remedies.

In plain wordsAn OD intervention is a planned action aimed at one diagnosed problem: a workshop, a survey, a redesign.

Exam definitionOD interventions are structured programmes, activities or techniques designed to manage change, improve performance and enhance employee well-being. A sound intervention is data-driven, participative and goal-oriented.

Interventions are grouped by the level they work on.

LevelIt targetsInterventions
IndividualSkills, mindset, behaviour, motivationCoaching and mentoring; training and development, such as a cyber-safety workshop for bank clerks
TeamGroup dynamics, collaboration, outputTeam building, such as an off-site retreat; role negotiation
OrganisationStrategy, structure, cultureStrategic planning, such as a five-year plan; structural redesign, such as flattening the hierarchy
ProcessSystems, workflows, decision-makingBusiness process re-engineering; process consultation

The main interventions, with an illustration for each:

InterventionWhat it isIllustration
Sensitivity trainingUnstructured group sessions (a T-group or laboratory) where members give and receive frank feedback on how they come across. It builds self-awareness and empathy.Managers from different branches join a residential lab and discuss how they affect one another
Team buildingStructured activities and retreats that build trust, clear roles and shared goals in a work teamThe merged department spends a day mapping who does which task
Process consultationA consultant watches how a group communicates, decides and handles conflict, and helps members see and fix it themselves (Edgar Schein, 1969)A consultant sits in the weekly meeting, then shows the team how decisions really get made
Survey feedbackA questionnaire goes to all; the results return to each work group, which discusses them and plans actionAn anonymous workload survey; each section reviews its own results
Structural redesignChanging roles, reporting lines or the grouping of jobs for efficiency and flexibilityOne head replaces two; subject teams replace departments
Organisational learningRoutines that share what people know and learn from mistakesMonthly lunch-and-learn talks; a review after each admission season
Role negotiationEach side writes what it wants the other to do more of, less of and keep doing, then they bargain a written agreement (Roger Harrison, 1972)Head office and a regional office settle who approves which expense
Business process re-engineering (BPR)Radical redesign of a process, starting from what the customer needs, to gain sharply in cost, quality, service and speed (Hammer and Champy, 1993)Admission papers move from six desks to one counter

BPR runs in five stages: map the current process, analyse it, find the improvement opportunities, design the future process map, and implement it with training and support.

OD uses a few tools. A tool gathers data, spreads skills or reinforces behaviour; interventions are built from them.

ToolUse
Surveys and questionnairesGather feedback from many people, such as an engagement survey
Focus groupsSmall-group discussion in depth, such as finding why staff resist a change
WorkshopsTrain or engage teams, such as a diversity and inclusion session
Job rotationMove people across jobs to widen skills, such as a marketing executive spending time in sales
Reward systemsReinforce desired behaviour, such as a bonus for high-performing teams

Older exam questions also list other techniques as OD interventions.

  • Managerial grid (Blake and Mouton): concern for production against concern for people; covered under leadership.
  • Management by objectives (Peter Drucker, 1954): managers and staff agree objectives and review results against them.
  • Brainstorming: free generation of ideas in a group, usually with criticism held back until later.
  • Quality circles: small voluntary groups of workers from one area who meet regularly to solve work problems; begun in Japan in the 1960s.
  • Transactional analysis: covered in the chapter on interpersonal behaviour.

Don't confuse sensitivity training with team building. Sensitivity training works on individuals' self-awareness in an open-ended group. Team building works on a real work team's task, roles and trust. Also, process consultation is not expert consulting: the consultant does not supply the answer but helps the group find its own.

Where it breaks. An intervention aimed at the wrong level wastes money: a retreat cannot fix a six-desk process. One-off events fade unless reinforced. A survey whose results are never shared teaches staff that their answers do not matter. Sensitivity training can be stressful, and what is learned may not carry back to the job. BPR has been criticised for serving as cover for cutting jobs.

In practice. Choose by the diagnosis, then by level, cost and readiness. Pilot first, and combine: survey feedback to find the problem, team building to work on it.

For exams. Match the intervention to its level and to its author: Schein for process consultation, Hammer and Champy for BPR. Expect a case where you pick the best fit.

Go deeper for practitioners

Chris Argyris and Donald Schön separated single-loop learning, which corrects an error within the current rules, from double-loop learning, which questions the rules and goals themselves. A review that only asks how to avoid late papers next year is single-loop. One that asks whether six desks should exist is double-loop. Peter Senge (1990) used the idea of a learning organisation for firms that do this routinely.

The T-group grew out of a training workshop that Lewin and his colleagues ran in 1946, a link back to the founder of the next concept.

A decision. A survey shows mistrust between two groups, and a redesign would also cut a post. Team building is cheap and quick. Redesign is lasting but threatens people. Which would you start with, and what would you tell the staff?

Level first: individual, team, organisation, process. Then pick the tool.

blocks.title: Lewin's model, benefits and challenges
blocks.html:
A bank branch has run on ledgers for twenty years. The new software goes live on Monday. A month later half the clerks still keep a paper register on the side. Installing a change does not make people adopt it, and Lewin's model shows why.

In plain wordsLewin said change has three stages: loosen the old ways, move to the new ones, then settle the new ones so they last.

Exam definitionKurt Lewin's three-stage model of planned change (1947) has three stages: unfreezing, changing (moving) and refreezing.

Lewin's leadership styles and his formula B = f(P, E) appear in other chapters. The change model is a separate part of his work.

StagePurposeThe branch (an illustration)
1 UnfreezePrepare people to accept the need: show why the old way no longer works and lower the fearThe manager shares queue times, error counts and customer complaints, and asks clerks what slows them down. She promises that nobody is penalised for mistakes during the learning weeks.
2 ChangeIntroduce the new behaviours, processes or tools, with training and supportClerks are trained in small batches. One trained colleague is placed at each counter as a helper. Old and new systems run together for a short period.
3 RefreezeReinforce the new behaviour until it becomes the normThe paper registers are retired. Targets and appraisal now use the new system's measures. Early adopters are recognised.

Lewin's model and the OD process run side by side, but they describe different things. The model describes what happens to people's habits. The OD process describes the consultant's work. Roughly, diagnosis and feedback help to unfreeze, implementation is the change, and reinforcement is refreezing.

Benefits and challenges of OD

BenefitsChallenges
Higher productivity, performance and innovationResistance, born of fear of the unknown
Better communication and decision-makingIt takes a long time and sustained effort
Greater adaptability to market shiftsImpact is hard to measure and to separate from other causes
Higher satisfaction and retentionIt needs committed top management
Stronger teamwork, morale and leadershipA temporary performance dip while people adjust
Better learning, and people aligned with strategyPoor communication can create mistrust

Don't confuse refreezing with freezing for ever. It means making the new way the normal way. The next change will need unfreezing again.

Where it breaks. Critics say the model is too simple and too linear. It pictures a stable organisation, disturbed once and then stable again; many organisations now change continuously, so there may be no steady state to refreeze into. It also says little about power, politics and culture, and it suits change led from the top. Some scholars argue that the three steps are a later simplification of Lewin's richer work on group dynamics, action research and force fields.

In practice. Spend the most effort on unfreezing. Many change programmes stumble because managers jump straight to training for people who do not yet see why. Plan the refreezing too: if appraisal and rewards still favour the old way, the old way returns.

For exams. Know the order and the standard examples: unfreezing, communicating poor performance data; changing, training in new software; refreezing, new KPIs and rewards aligned with the changed goals. Memory aid: prepare, implement, stabilise.

Go deeper for practitioners

Lewin's force-field analysis pictures any present level as a balance between driving forces that push for change and restraining forces that push against it. Change happens when the balance tips.

Unfreezing means tipping the balance, by adding driving forces, removing restraining ones, or both. The advice to remove restraints first is the more useful half of the analysis.

A decision. The branch head has a head-office target to push. Clerks say they fear errors and have no time to practise. Does she add a stricter deadline, or free two afternoons a week for practice? Which force is she changing?

Unfreeze, change, refreeze: prepare, implement, stabilise.

chapters.title: Industrial Relations, Disputes and Grievances
chapters.scope: What industrial relations is and aims at, the main approaches to it, how industrial disputes arise, take shape and are prevented or settled, and how employee grievances are handled.

blocks.title: What industrial relations is
blocks.html:
At an auto-parts plant in Pune, the night shift refuses to start after a supervisor humiliates a worker in front of the line. Within hours the management, the union office-bearers and the labour department are all involved. Industrial relations is the study of how such situations are prevented and handled.

In plain wordsIndustrial relations (IR) is the web of dealings between the people who run a workplace, the people who work in it, their unions and the government.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: industrial relations is the management of relationships among employers, employees, trade unions and the government, with the aim of industrial harmony and productivity.

"Industry" here has a wide meaning: any productive activity. It covers farming, plantations and mining as well as manufacturing, construction, trade, transport and banking. IR is therefore not only about factories.

Four parties take part. Employers and their managers run the work. Employees do it. Trade unions speak for groups of workers. The government makes the rules and often steps in when the others cannot agree.

IR covers the terms of employment and working conditions, collective bargaining, grievance handling, conflict resolution and workers' share in management. Trade unions and bargaining, labour welfare, and wages and profit sharing have their own chapters (Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining; Labour Welfare and Social Security; Wage Determination, Profit Sharing and Payment-by-Results Plans). This chapter covers the approaches to IR, industrial disputes and grievances.

Five objectives. Most exam lists boil down to these.

ObjectiveWhat it means in practice
Healthy relationshipsTrust and open communication reduce suspicion and strengthen industrial peace.
Prevent and resolve disputesTimely grievance redressal, and talks, mediation or arbitration before anyone strikes.
Welfare and productivitySafer, better working conditions raise satisfaction, cut absenteeism, turnover and accidents, and so lift output.
Limited government interventionEmployers and workers settle matters through their own rules and forums, so outside interference is rarely needed.
Industrial democracyWorkers have a voice in decisions, through joint councils, committees and shared target setting.

Suppose the Pune plant starts a monthly joint committee of managers and workers' representatives, answers every written complaint within a week, and reviews shop-floor safety twice a year. Each step serves one objective: trust, prevention, welfare, self-regulation and voice. The figures are illustrative.

Don't confuse industrial relations with human resource management. HRM (see the chapter Human Resource Management) deals with each employee: hiring, training, appraisal and pay. IR deals with the collective side: groups of workers, their unions, employers and the state. In many firms one department does both.

Where it breaks. "Harmony" is an aim, not a fact. Some writers argue that employers and workers really do have different interests, so peace needs bargaining and not only goodwill. The next block shows how the approaches disagree. Also, "limited government intervention" is an ideal: India has extensive labour law, and the parties often settle disputes only because the law gives them a deadline or a forum.

In practice. A manager who builds a working grievance route, a regular talking forum and fair rules rarely needs the labour department. Disputes that reach it usually started as small complaints that nobody answered.

For exams. Learn the four parties, the aim (harmony and productivity) and the five objectives. Questions also ask which theorist goes with which approach, which the next block covers.

Four parties, one aim: harmony and productivity.

blocks.title: Approaches to industrial relations
blocks.html:
A union leader asks for a wage revision, and two managers react. One says, "We are one team, so why is anyone organising against us?" The other says, "Workers and owners want different things, so let us bargain." Each manager holds a theory of industrial relations. The theory shapes what each does next.

In plain wordsAn approach to IR is a way of seeing the workplace. It tells you whether conflict is a fault, a normal fact or a product of society, and so what to do about it.

Exam definitionApproaches to industrial relations are schools of thought that explain employer-employee relations and industrial conflict. The main ones are unitary, pluralist, Marxist, systems, Oxford, industrial sociology, action frame of reference, human relations and Gandhian.

The first three are broad views of conflict. The rest are named after thinkers, and exams ask you to match them.

ApproachThinkerCore idea
UnitarynoneThe organisation is one team with one source of authority, the management. Conflict is rare and comes from poor communication or troublemakers. Critics call it manipulative.
PluralistnoneThe organisation holds several groups with different aims. Conflict between management and workers is normal and rational, so it is managed through bargaining.
MarxistnoneConflict comes from class division in a capitalist society. Workplace disputes are one part of it.
SystemsJohn T. Dunlop, Industrial Relations Systems (1958)IR is a system of actors, contexts and ideology that produces rules for the workplace.
OxfordAllan FlandersIR is the study of the institutions that regulate jobs, and of the substantive and procedural rules they make.
Industrial sociologyG. MargerisonIR is studied as social behaviour: how people act in groups at work, including their conflicts.
Action frame of referenceDavid Silverman (1970)People are actors who give their own meaning to the situation and act on it. Employers and unions pursue their own ends and settle matters by bargaining.
Human relationsElton Mayo, with Roethlisberger, Whyte and HomansUnmet human and social needs cause trouble. Good supervision, communication and participation raise morale.
GandhianM. K. GandhiPeace rests on trusteeship, non-violence and moral persuasion.

Dunlop's system. Dunlop's three sets of inputs are the actors, the contexts and the ideology. The actors are managers and their representatives, workers and their representatives, and government agencies. The contexts are technology, market or budget pressures, and the distribution of power in society. The ideology is the shared set of beliefs that holds the system together. The output is a web of rules: substantive rules (pay, hours) and procedural rules (how rules are made and applied).

The Gandhian approach. Gandhi held that owners should treat their wealth as a trust for society. He preferred peaceful persuasion and arbitration to confrontation, and allowed a strike only as a last resort, for a just cause and without violence. Human relations draws on the Hawthorne studies, which the chapter Organisational Behaviour: Significance and Theories introduces. Keith Davis defined human relations as the integration of people into a work situation that motivates them to work together productively, cooperatively and with economic, psychological and social satisfaction.

Don't confuse Dunlop's systems approach with the Oxford approach. Both stress rules. Dunlop builds a whole system around the rules: actors, contexts and ideology. Flanders looks at the institutions that make the rules, above all collective bargaining. Also, study material sometimes calls the action frame the "action theory" or "social action" approach. It is one approach, credited to Silverman.

Where it breaks. The approaches are lenses, not rival laws. The unitary view ignores real differences of interest. The pluralist view assumes the two sides bargain on fairly equal terms. The Marxist view says little about day-to-day bargaining. Human relations is criticised for treating pay and power disputes as problems of feeling. Trusteeship depends on the owner's goodwill, which no one can compel.

In practice. A manager with a unitary view reads every union demand as disloyalty. One with a pluralist view expects demands, prepares for them and bargains. Most managers in practice use a mix.

For exams. Match the names: Dunlop with systems, Flanders with Oxford, Margerison with industrial sociology, Silverman with the action frame, Mayo with human relations. Dunlop's system has actors, contexts, ideology and rules; inputs and outputs are not among those elements.

Go deeper for practitioners

Indian exam lists often add the V. V. Giri approach. It prefers settling disputes by mutual talks, collective bargaining and voluntary arbitration, and opposes compulsory adjudication because it weakens the unions' own strength. It sits close to the Gandhian approach in spirit.

The next block shows these ideas in action: the legal machinery for disputes mixes both. It offers conciliation and voluntary arbitration, which are Giri-like, and adjudication, which is imposed.

Unitary one team, pluralist many groups, Marxist class.

blocks.title: Industrial disputes and settlement
blocks.html:
A Pune plant's union asks for a higher bonus. Management says margins are thin. Talks stall, and the shop floor starts to talk of stopping work. What can each side do, and where does the law come in?

In plain wordsAn industrial dispute is a disagreement about work that two sides cannot settle. It may be about pay, jobs or working conditions.

Exam definitionUnder the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an industrial dispute is any dispute or difference between employers and employers, or between employers and workmen, or between workmen and workmen, which is connected with the employment or non-employment, or the terms of employment, or the conditions of labour, of any person.

Note the three pairings. Employer against employer: two firms disagree over a common wage settlement. Employer against workers: the usual case. Worker against worker: two groups quarrel over seniority or over which union represents them.

Law today. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 consolidates the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, and speaks of "workers" where the old Act said "workmen". Older exam questions still use the 1947 Act's terms, so learn them. Check the Code's current text for notice periods and thresholds.

Causes. They fall into two groups.

Economic causesNon-economic causes
Wages, bonus and dearness allowanceRecognition of trade unions
Conditions of work and employment, working hoursVictimisation: punishing a worker for union activity or complaining
Leave and holidays with payIll-treatment by supervisors
Unjust dismissal or retrenchmentSympathy with workers elsewhere, and political causes

Forms of industrial action. Each side has a pressure tool. Workers use the strike, gherao and picketing. Employers use the lockout.

FormWho actsWhat happens
StrikeWorkersA group of workers stop work together to press their demands.
LockoutEmployerThe employer shuts the workplace, or refuses to employ workers, until they accept its terms.
GheraoWorkersWorkers surround managers and stop them leaving. Confining people against their will can break criminal law.
PicketingWorkersWorkers stand at the gate to persuade others not to work, and to draw public attention. Peaceful picketing is usually treated as lawful; violence is not.

Textbooks list several kinds of strike.

KindMeaning
Economic strikeWorkers stop work because talks on pay, benefits or conditions failed.
Unfair labour practice strikeA strike to protest illegal conduct by the employer.
Sympathy strikeOne union strikes in support of another union's strike.
General strikeWorkers across many unions in a region or industry stop work together.
Wildcat strikeA sudden strike without the union's approval, often while an agreement is in force.
Sit-down strikeWorkers stay at their workplace but refuse to work. Also called a stay-in, tools-down or pen-down strike.
Go-slowWorkers keep working but deliberately cut output. Textbooks list it among strikes.

The law's frame. The law treats strikes and lockouts as regulated actions, not unlimited rights. Rules on notice and on timing apply, and they are stricter for essential services. Whether a strike is lawful depends on whether those rules were followed.

Preventing and settling. The aim is to stop disputes before they reach a strike.

A works committee is a standing forum of employer and worker representatives in larger establishments. It sorts out small differences and keeps relations good. It prevents disputes; it does not settle them. In conciliation a neutral officer helps the parties find an agreement but cannot force one. In adjudication a labour court or industrial tribunal hears both sides and gives a binding decision. In voluntary arbitration the parties choose their own arbitrator and agree to accept the decision.

Don't confuse collective bargaining with settlement machinery. Collective bargaining is a method of negotiation: the two sides talk directly, and no neutral decides. Conciliation, adjudication and voluntary arbitration are the machinery for settling a dispute. The works committee is preventive machinery. The chapter Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining teaches bargaining itself.

Where it breaks. The categories overlap. A sympathy strike can also be a general strike. Statutory routes can take long, and a worker who feels ignored may turn to quicker, unofficial action. Strikes and lockouts cost both sides: the workers lose pay, the employer loses output and customers.

In practice. Settle early. A manager who reads the causes of a dispute, economic or not, and answers them before positions harden often avoids the ladder altogether.

For exams. Learn the three-sided definition, the two groups of causes, the forms of action and the four machinery terms. A recurring question asks which items are settlement machinery; do not count collective bargaining or the works committee.

Prevent, conciliate, then decide.

blocks.title: Grievance management
blocks.html:
A machine operator in Pune is denied the overtime pay that the company policy promises. His supervisor says, "Later." A month later the operator tells his union representative, and three more operators say the same thing. A complaint nobody answered has become a collective problem.

In plain wordsA grievance is an employee's complaint that something at work is unfair. It may be right or wrong, but it matters either way.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a grievance is a sense of dissatisfaction or injustice about something connected with one's job. It may or may not be justified, and it usually reflects the gap between what the employee expects and what the employee gets.

Grievances matter because they lower motivation and performance and damage the work climate. Handled early, they cost little. Ignored, they feed disputes.

Types. Grievances are grouped by who is affected.

TypeWho is affectedExampleUsually raised by
IndividualOne employeeDemotion based on bias, unpaid salary, harassmentThe employee
GroupA team or group in the same wayNone of the team gets the overtime bonus the policy promises, or unsafe conditionsThe group, or its representative
Policy or unionMany or all employees, or how a policy or agreement is readA dispute over how a policy or agreement should be interpretedThe union

The five-step process. A good handling procedure follows a fixed order, so that every complaint gets the same fair treatment.

  1. Acknowledge. Register the complaint, in writing even if it was spoken. Show the employee they were heard, and keep the matter confidential as far as possible.
  2. Investigate. Collect facts, documents and witness statements. Hear both sides. Check the case against policy and the law.
  3. Communicate. Tell the people involved what is happening and when to expect an answer. Use neutral words that calm the matter rather than inflame it.
  4. Resolve. Decide promptly and fairly, in line with policy and labour law. Bring in a mediator if the two sides are stuck.
  5. Document and follow up. Record what was decided and why. Later, check that the problem is really closed and that the employee faced no retaliation.

Why open procedures matter. A procedure that employees can see and trust brings problems up while they are small. It builds trust, and the records show managers where policies cause repeated trouble. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 also requires larger establishments to have a grievance redressal committee; check its current text for the details.

Don't confuse a grievance with an industrial dispute. A grievance is the employee's complaint, raised inside the organisation. It usually becomes an industrial dispute when it stays unresolved and is taken up as a difference between the employer and the workers, often through a union. Nor is it whistleblowing, which reports wrongdoing that harms others; see Organisational Justice and Whistleblowing.

Where it breaks. A procedure that exists only on paper is worse than none. Employees stay silent if they fear retaliation, if the supervisor who caused the problem decides the case, or if answers take months.

In practice. People accept a disappointing result more easily when the process is fair and they were treated with respect. The chapter Organisational Justice and Whistleblowing explains why. Whether employees dare to complain also depends on culture and on how freely information flows; see Organisational Culture and Climate and Communication.

For exams. Know the definition, the three types and the five steps in order: acknowledge, investigate, communicate, resolve, document and follow up.

Go deeper for practitioners

Three night-shift operators tell a supervisor, one by one, that a promised shift allowance was left out of their pay. Treated as three individual complaints, they get three separate answers and a sense of being brushed off. Treated as one group grievance, the supervisor registers it once, checks the payroll rule once, and gives one clear answer to all three.

The decision to treat it as a group case is step 1. It also leads to an earlier fix at step 4, and the record at step 5 helps HR check whether other shifts are missing the same allowance.

Acknowledge, investigate, communicate, resolve, document.

chapters.title: Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining
chapters.scope: What trade unions are and want, how collective bargaining works from preparation to renewal, the types of bargaining, and the common terms and strike kinds.

blocks.title: Trade unions
blocks.html:
Forty workers in a packaging unit near Pune each ask the owner for a raise. He can refuse each one, or replace whoever keeps asking. If all forty act together, he cannot wave them away so easily. A trade union is the way workers act together.

In plain wordsA trade union is a group of workers who join so that they deal with the employer as one body, not one by one.

Exam definitionA trade union is an organised group of workers formed to protect and promote their collective interests, such as wages, working hours, job security and safe working conditions.

One worker has little power against an employer who controls jobs and pay. A union gives workers a shared voice, information about their rights, and protection in employment matters. It also stands between workers and management and carries messages both ways.

Objectives. Unions pursue four kinds of aim.

ObjectiveWhat the union seeksExample
EconomicFair wages, bonus and allowances; reasonable hours and overtime pay; retirement benefits and insuranceDemanding a higher festival bonus
ProtectiveProtection from exploitation, unfair dismissal and harassment; job security; safe conditionsDefending a worker sacked without a hearing
PoliticalInfluence over labour laws; support for pro-worker legislation; often links with political partiesCampaigning for a change in a labour law
SocialAdult education, child welfare, awareness of legal rights, medical camps, community welfareA health camp for members' families

Types of union. Two different questions sort unions. The first asks who may join. The second asks what kind of job members do.

TypeWho belongsExample
Craft unionWorkers with the same craft, skill or occupation, whatever industry they work inElectricians from many factories in one union
Industrial unionWorkers of one industry, whatever their craftEveryone in a sugar mill, from weighbridge clerk to fitter
General unionWorkers of any craft or industry, often within a city or regionA city-wide union open to all workers
Blue-collar unionWorkers in operative jobs, usually running machines in production and allied departmentsMachine operators in an auto-parts plant
White-collar unionOffice and service staff on desk jobs or counter work: clerks, supervisors, administrators, professionalsBank clerks and officers

Some books also list a "labour union", open to all workers whatever their skill or industry, on the idea that all workers share a common status and need to help each other. Treat it as a general union.

Central organisations. Unions in a workplace often join national federations. Well-known Indian ones are the Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC), the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), the Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) and the Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU). Several have traditionally been linked to political parties, which is the political objective at work.

The law. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 was India's main law on unions. It let a union register and gain a legal identity, and it protected registered unions from some criminal and civil liability for acts done in a trade dispute. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 now consolidates that Act with the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The four labour codes took effect on 21 November 2025, and the formal repeal of the three older Acts awaited a separate notification when last checked. Older exam questions still use the 1926 and 1947 Acts' terms.

Don't confuse a craft union with an industrial union. A craft union groups people by skill across industries. An industrial union groups people by industry across skills. Likewise, "blue-collar" and "white-collar" describe the job, not the membership rule.

Where it breaks. Several unions in one workplace can compete for members, and rivalry weakens the workers' common position. Links to political parties can pull a union towards goals that are not the members' own. Many workers are in the unorganised sector, where unions are rare, so a union speaks for far fewer workers than the whole workforce.

For exams. Learn the four objectives (economic, protective, political, social), the types and the difference between craft and industrial unions. Expect a question on the Trade Unions Act, 1926.

Economic, protective, political, social: craft by skill, industrial by industry, general for all.

blocks.title: Collective bargaining
blocks.html:
The forty workers now have a union, and the owner has agreed to meet it. Who sits at the table, what do they discuss, and what makes the outcome last? That meeting is collective bargaining.

In plain wordsCollective bargaining is employer and workers' representatives talking until they agree on the terms of work, so management does not set the terms alone.

Exam definitionCollective bargaining is a negotiation between employee representatives, usually a trade union, and the employer to determine terms and conditions of employment such as wages, benefits, job security and working conditions.

Four features mark it. It is collective: a group bargains, not an individual. It has two sides, the employer and the workers' representatives. It is a continuing process, because agreements expire and are renewed. And it rests on give and take: each side wants an agreement more than a breakdown. Its purpose is to reach terms both sides can accept, and so to prevent conflict before it starts.

Five stages. A bargaining round moves through these steps and then starts again.

  • Preparation. Both sides collect facts, such as wages elsewhere in the industry, productivity and what the firm can afford, and decide their goals and limits.
  • Negotiation. The sides exchange offers and counter-offers and look for terms both accept.
  • Agreement. Once there is consensus, the terms are written down and signed as the collective bargaining agreement (CBA).
  • Implementation. The employer applies the terms and the union watches that it does. If the employer does not, grievances and strikes follow.
  • Follow-up and renegotiation. Both sides review how the agreement worked. As it nears its end, new demands are prepared.

The agreement. A CBA runs for a fixed period, often a few years. Whether a court will enforce it depends on the country's law. In India, under the 1947 Act, a settlement reached with a conciliation officer's help binds all workers of the establishment, while a direct agreement outside conciliation binds only the parties who signed it. Bank wages are an example of industry-wide bargaining: the Indian Banks' Association and the bank unions negotiate settlements for the whole sector.

Levels. Bargaining can happen at the plant (one firm or factory), at the industry (many firms together, through an employers' association and unions) or at the national level. Plant bargaining fits local conditions. Industry bargaining gives one rule to all firms, so no firm can undercut the rest on pay.

Don't confuse collective bargaining with worker participation. In bargaining, two sides negotiate the terms of work, and each protects its own interest. In participation, workers share in decisions about running the work, through works committees or joint councils. The industrial relations chapter treats participation and industrial democracy. Also note that some textbooks give six or more steps, adding items such as ratification by union members. The five stages above are the standard set.

Where it breaks. The result depends on each side's strength. A split union, or one that cannot back its demands with a strike threat, bargains from weakness. An employer who refuses to talk, or talks without data, stalls the process.

For exams. Know the definition, the five stages in order and the CBA. When a dispute arises, the neighbouring chapter on industrial relations covers strikes, lockouts and settlement.

Prepare, negotiate, agree, implement, review.

blocks.title: Types of bargaining
blocks.html:
A textile mill in trouble asks its workers for a wage freeze. A growing plant offers a bonus tied to output. A union asks for pay, safer machines and job security in one package. All three are collective bargaining, yet the talks are very different.

In plain wordsBargaining types describe the style of the talks or what the deal is about: fighting over a fixed sum, or looking for a gain both sides share.

Exam definitionDistributive bargaining is a win-lose negotiation over a fixed resource. Integrative bargaining seeks win-win solutions that serve both parties' interests.

TypeCore ideaIllustration
DistributiveWin-lose: a fixed sum, so one side's gain is the other's lossThe union asks for a 12% pay rise and the employer offers 5%. They settle at 8%. Each extra rupee for workers is a rupee less for the firm.
IntegrativeWin-win: both sides work on shared interests to make the gain biggerA bottling plant and its union cut waste together and share the saving as a bonus.
ConcessionaryThe union gives up benefits during financial stress to protect jobsA struggling mill's union accepts a one-year wage freeze in return for no layoffs.
ProductivityPay and benefits are tied to gains in efficiency or outputA bonus is paid when the line's output rises above an agreed level.
CompositeOne bargain covers many issues, not a single demandA settlement on job security, working hours and safety together with pay.

Don't confuse the types with each other. Distributive and integrative describe the style of talks. Concessionary, productivity and composite describe what the deal is about. A productivity deal can be reached in an integrative spirit, because both sides gain from higher output. A concessionary deal is usually distributive in feel, because the union gives and the firm keeps.

Benefits. Workers can win better pay and benefits than they would alone. They gain a say in decisions that affect them, which is a form of workplace democracy. Talking early prevents disputes, so there are fewer strikes and legal fights. Trust and cooperation improve, and so does morale.

Challenges.

  • Multiplicity of unions. When several unions work in one firm, each claims to speak for the workers. The employer does not know whom to deal with, and bargaining power is weakened. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 tackles this by providing for a sole negotiating union, or a council of unions where none has enough support.
  • Lack of unity. Rival unions compete for members, and workers' demands are split.
  • Employer resistance. Some employers avoid or delay talks.
  • Legal limits. Unions must meet registration and recognition rules, and delays in enforcing agreements weaken their value.
  • Globalisation. Outsourcing, contract labour and automation move work away from the shop floor and make it harder to keep members.

Where it breaks. The five labels overlap, so a real negotiation often mixes them. Distributive bargaining also leaves a bad mood behind, which can hurt the next round.

In practice. A manager preparing for talks should list the interests behind each demand, not only the demand. A worker asking for pay may really want security, and security may cost the firm less than pay.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. A pump maker in Coimbatore (an illustration) has lost two large orders. Management proposes a one-year wage freeze or 60 job cuts. The union fears the freeze will quietly become permanent.

This begins as concessionary bargaining. The union can turn it into an integrative bargain by asking for something back: a written promise of no layoffs, a date on which pay is restored, and a bonus linked to profit when orders recover. Management gains cost relief and a calmer shop floor, and the workers gain security. What would you ask for if you were the union, and what would you refuse to give?

Distributive wins and loses; integrative wins together.

blocks.title: Common terms and strike kinds
blocks.html:
A new factory hires 200 workers. Must they join the union? Can the owner hire someone who refuses? And when talks fail, who decides? Each answer is a term in the language of bargaining.

In plain wordsThese terms say whether workers must be in a union, how a stuck dispute gets settled, and what kind of strike has happened.

Exam definitionArbitration is the settlement of a dispute by a neutral third party, whose decision the parties have agreed, or are required, to accept.

TermMeaning
Closed shopThe employer may hire only union members. In one form, workers must be members before they are hired.
Open shopWorkers choose freely whether to join a union.
Agency shopWorkers need not join, but all must pay the union a fee for bargaining on their behalf.
ArbitrationA neutral third party hears both sides and decides when talks have failed. It is voluntary when both sides agree to it.
Grievance procedureA formal, stepwise way to settle a worker's complaint, usually starting with the immediate supervisor.

Strikes and lockouts are the weapons of last resort. The industrial relations chapter covers them and how disputes are settled. Here the question is only what each kind of strike means.

Kind of strikeWhat it is
Economic strikeWorkers strike because they and the employer failed to agree on the terms of a contract, such as wages, benefits and other conditions of employment.
Unfair labour practice strikeWorkers strike to protest illegal conduct by the employer.
Wildcat strikeA sudden strike without the union's approval, such as one that breaks out while an agreement is still running.
Sympathy strikeOne union strikes in support of another union's strike.

These four names come from the classification used in labour-relations textbooks. Indian law sorts strikes differently, for example as legal or illegal, so use these terms as the exam's vocabulary.

Don't confuse an economic strike with an unfair labour practice strike. An economic strike is about what the workers will be paid or given. An unfair labour practice strike is about whether the employer broke the law. Also, a wildcat strike lacks union approval, while a sympathy strike is for another union's cause and may well be approved.

Where it breaks. A closed shop forces workers to join a union to get a job, so many countries restrict or ban it. Arbitration ends a stalemate, but it hands the outcome to a stranger, and neither side may like the award.

For exams. Matching questions pair a strike name with its meaning. Learn each in a few words: terms (economic), employer's illegal act (unfair labour practice), no union approval (wildcat), another union's cause (sympathy).

Economic: terms. Unfair practice: employer's wrong. Wildcat: no approval. Sympathy: for another.

chapters.title: Labour Welfare and Social Security
chapters.scope: How employers, unions and the state care for workers beyond wages: the meaning and theories of labour welfare, the types of welfare facility, and the idea and Indian instruments of social security.

blocks.title: Labour welfare and its theories
blocks.html:
A garment factory in Tiruppur builds a clean canteen and a rest room. Ask five owners why they would, and you may hear five answers: the law demands it, it is a duty, it keeps workers calm, it looks good, it raises output. Each answer is one theory of labour welfare.

In plain wordsLabour welfare is the care for workers' health, comfort and living conditions that goes beyond their wages.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: labour welfare means the services, facilities and amenities provided for workers, at or near the workplace, by employers, trade unions, government and other bodies, over and above wages.

The words over and above wages matter. A canteen, a crèche or a first-aid room is welfare. The wage packet is not. The providers are many: the employer, the union, the government, and voluntary organisations.

Why it is done. The aims differ for each side.

  • Workers: better health, safer and more comfortable work, and a better life for their families.
  • Employers: higher morale and motivation, a workforce that stays longer, and better relations with workers.
  • Both: a calmer workplace, with fewer quarrels over working conditions.

In the HR functions, safety and welfare is the "protect" function (see the chapter on human resource management).

Seven theories. The theories do not describe seven kinds of welfare. They describe seven motives, seven reasons an employer gives welfare at all.

TheoryWhy the employer gives welfareWelfare is seen as
PolicingEmployers will not act unless forced, and they can exploit workers. So the state steps in and fixes a minimum standard.A legal minimum
ReligiousReligious belief moves the employer, who hopes for merit in this life or the next.A good deed
PhilanthropicLove of mankind and compassion for workers' suffering. Early welfare work in the industrial age came from such people.Charity
Paternalistic or trusteeshipThe employer holds the business in trust for workers and society, and looks after workers as a guardian looks after wards.A guardian's duty
PlacatingWorkers are organised and demanding. Timely welfare gestures calm them before they press further.A peace offering
Public relationsWelfare builds goodwill among workers and with the public, and projects a good image.An advertisement
FunctionalA healthy, contented worker is more productive, so welfare protects and builds efficiency.An investment in output

Law, faith, love, guardianship, calm, image, output.

Don't confuse the look-alikes. In the policing theory the "police" is the state, not the employer. Placating aims to calm organised workers; public relations aims at the firm's image with workers and the public. The trusteeship theory is related to Gandhi's idea of trusteeship, but the two are not the same. Gandhi's idea is wider: those who hold wealth should treat it as held for society. The welfare theory is narrower and adds the picture of workers as wards who cannot manage their own interests.

Where it breaks. The theories describe motives, not rules, and one firm can act from several at once. Three of them (religious, philanthropic, paternalistic) treat welfare as a favour from the employer. Workers are then receivers of kindness, not people with a rightful claim to a share of what their work creates. A favour can also be withdrawn when times are hard.

For exams. Expect a description to be given and the theory asked for, or the seven names to be listed. Know the definition, the words "over and above wages", and the providers.

Go deeper for practitioners

Motive shows in how a scheme is run. A scheme announced a week before wage talks can be read as placating, whatever the intention. A scheme designed without asking workers can feel like a favour, which is the paternalistic pattern. The remedy comes from procedural justice (see the chapter on organisational justice): let workers help choose the facilities and see how the money is spent.

The functional theory is the easiest to defend to a finance head. But if welfare is justified only by the output it brings, it is the first thing cut when output falls. Firms that also see welfare as a duty to people tend to protect it better.

How unions bargain over such matters is taught in the chapters on industrial relations, and on trade unions and collective bargaining.

blocks.title: Types of welfare facilities
blocks.html:
A large factory has a canteen inside the gate, a housing colony outside it, a cricket tournament each winter, and a credit society that the workers run themselves. Some of these the law requires; others exist only because someone chose to start them. To manage them, an HR manager needs a way to sort them.

In plain wordsWelfare facilities are sorted in two ways: where they are provided, and who provides or requires them.

Exam definitionA standard textbook classification has five types. Intra-mural facilities are provided inside the workplace. Extra-mural facilities are provided outside it. Statutory facilities are required by law. Voluntary facilities are provided by the employer by choice. Mutual facilities are organised by the workers themselves.

The first pair sorts by place. The second group sorts by who: the law, the employer, or the workers. The two ways cross each other, so one facility can have a label from each.

TypeSorted byExamples
Intra-muralPlace: inside the workplaceDrinking water, washing facilities, canteen, rest rooms, crèche, first-aid room, good lighting, safe layout of machines
Extra-muralPlace: outside the workplaceHousing, recreation and sports, education for workers and their children
StatutoryLaw: the employer must provideThe basic amenities that labour law lists, such as drinking water, first aid and a canteen
VoluntaryEmployer's own choiceA staff sports club, scholarships for workers' children, subsidised transport
MutualWorkers' own effortA credit society or a consumer store run by the workers or their union

The law's list. The Factories Act has long required factories to provide basic amenities such as drinking water, washing facilities, a canteen, a crèche, rest rooms and first aid. Which factories must provide which amenity depends on the law's conditions, such as size, so read the current text before applying it. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, one of the four labour codes in force from 21 November 2025, now consolidates the Factories Act with other laws on safety and working conditions. Older exam questions still use the Factories Act's terms.

Sorting one factory. The canteen is intra-mural and statutory. The staff cricket tournament is extra-mural and voluntary. The workers' credit society is mutual, and the employer has little part in it. A housing colony is extra-mural, and voluntary unless a law requires it.

Don't confuse place with provider. "Intra-mural" and "extra-mural" say where. "Statutory", "voluntary" and "mutual" say who. Notes sometimes imply that all extra-mural facilities are voluntary. That is usually true, but not always: the law for plantations, for example, requires employers to provide housing. Voluntary and mutual also differ: voluntary comes from the employer, mutual from the workers.

Where it breaks. The labels overlap, so exam answers and real audits both need a clear rule: place first, then provider. The law sets only a floor, and a legal duty on paper is not a facility in practice. Voluntary facilities depend on the employer's goodwill and may shrink in a bad year.

In practice. List every facility and tag it twice. Check the statutory ones first, because those are duties. Then ask workers which voluntary ones they value, so the money goes where it helps.

For exams. Know the five types, one or two examples of each, and that statutory facilities cannot be ignored. Expect "give two examples of intra-mural facilities" and "distinguish statutory from voluntary".

blocks.title: Social security in India
blocks.html:
A packaging worker falls ill and loses three months of wages. A woman worker is about to have a child. A driver reaches 60 with no income. Wages cover the days a person works; they do not cover the breaks in work that life brings.

In plain wordsSocial security is a safety net. It gives money or medical care when a worker cannot earn, because of sickness, childbirth, injury, old age or unemployment.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: social security is the protection that society provides, through public arrangements, against economic distress. The distress follows when earnings stop or fall because of sickness, maternity, employment injury, old age, unemployment and similar risks.

Welfare and social security overlap but differ. Welfare is mostly facilities and services at or near work, and much of it is voluntary. Social security protects income and health against the big risks of a working life, through laws and funds.

The Indian instruments. India has no single scheme. It has a set of instruments, each aimed at one risk.

InstrumentMain riskPurpose
Provident fundOld ageRetirement savings built from contributions by both employee and employer during working life
Employees' state insuranceSickness, maternity, employment injuryMedical care and cash benefits for insured employees
GratuityEnd of long serviceA lump sum that the employer pays in recognition of long service
Maternity benefitChildbirthPaid leave and medical care for women employees around childbirth
Employee compensationInjury, disease or death caused by workThe employer pays the worker or the family (see the chapter on compensation management)

The Code today. The Code on Social Security, 2020 came into force on 21 November 2025. It consolidates the older social security laws, including those behind the five instruments above, into one Code. It also reaches gig and platform workers, whom the older laws did not name. The chapter on compensation management already notes this for the Employees' Compensation Act. Older exam questions still use the names of the old Acts, so learn both.

Don't confuse the provident fund with gratuity. The provident fund is built from contributions by the employee and the employer. Gratuity is paid by the employer alone, as a reward for long service. Both are paid at the end of employment, but they are different instruments with different sources.

Where it breaks. These instruments reach workers according to the kind and size of the employer and to formal employment. Many Indian workers are in the informal economy, and for them the gaps are wide. The Code tries to narrow this, but coverage on paper is not yet coverage in practice.

In practice. HR checks that every eligible employee is enrolled, that contributions are deposited on time, and that records are complete. A late deposit or a missing record can cost an employee a benefit and the employer a penalty.

For exams. Match each instrument to its risk, and know that the Code on Social Security, 2020 consolidates the older laws. Expect "distinguish labour welfare from social security".

chapters.title: Wage Determination, Profit Sharing and Payment-by-Results Plans
chapters.scope: How wages are set and judged, the main wage theories, profit sharing, and the payment-by-results plans that go beyond the classic time-saved plans.

blocks.title: Wage, salary and the wage concepts
blocks.html:
A packer in a Pune plant is paid by the day. A clerk at a bank branch is paid by the month. Both hear the words "minimum wage", and a union leader asks for a "living wage". The terms sound alike, but each marks a different level of pay.

In plain wordsA wage is pay counted by the hour, day or week. A salary is a fixed sum for the month or year, whatever hours are worked.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a wage is the pay of workers engaged on an hourly, daily or weekly basis, and it varies with the physical and mental demands of the job. A salary is the pay of employees engaged on a monthly or annual basis, irrespective of the hours put in.

Indian pay debates use three wage concepts, drawn from the report of the Committee on Fair Wages of the late 1940s. They form a ladder, and each step is higher than the one before.

ConceptWhat it must coverWhat limits it
Minimum wageThe worker's family needs, and the efficiency of the worker: food, clothing and shelter, plus some education, medical care and amenitiesNot the industry's capacity to pay: it is owed regardless
Fair wageMore than the minimum wage, but less than the living wageThe minimum wage below; the industry's capacity to pay above
Living wageThe essentials, plus frugal comfort: children's education, protection against ill health, essential social needs, and insurance against misfortunes, including old ageIt is an aim, not a legal floor

A fair wage depends on four things: the productivity of labour, the rates paid in the same or nearby places, the level and sharing of national income, and the industry's place in the economy.

What moves the wage a firm actually pays. The three concepts say what a wage should be. In practice an employer weighs eight things.

  • Ability to pay. Profitable firms can pay more; loss-making firms cannot.
  • Supply of and demand for labour. Scarce skills cost more.
  • The prevailing rate. Firms follow the going rate in their industry and area, to hold on to staff and to attract new ones.
  • Cost of living. Pay is adjusted for price rises. Dearness allowance does this in India, and an escalator clause in a contract does it automatically.
  • The living-wage idea. Employers prefer to pay for contribution, not need, and a family budget is open to argument.
  • Productivity. Output per worker-hour reflects machines, methods and management, not effort alone.
  • Union bargaining power. Generally, the stronger the union, the higher the wage.
  • Job requirements. Harder jobs pay more. Job evaluation ranks them (see Job Analysis, Evaluation and Design).

Don't confuse the wage concepts with the wage theories. The three concepts say what a wage ought to cover and are used in law and in awards. The theories, in the next concept, try to explain what actually sets wages. Note too that a theory's "subsistence wage" is not the "minimum wage": the minimum wage also covers efficiency, some education and medical care.

Where it breaks. Costing "needs" is a judgement. Which needs count, and for how many dependants? Capacity to pay is also disputed, since employers and unions read the same accounts differently. A higher floor helps those who keep their jobs, but a floor above what a small firm can pay may cost jobs or push work out of the formal sector. Economists debate how much.

In India. The Code on Wages, 2019 came into force on 21 November 2025 with the other labour codes. It consolidates four older laws, on payment of wages, minimum wages, payment of bonus and equal remuneration. Older exam questions still use those Acts' names. In concept, the law fixes a minimum wage that must be paid, and the Code adds a floor wage as a base below which minimum wages are not set. Rates change, so this chapter gives none.

For exams. Remember the order: minimum, fair, living. The fair wage lies between them, and its upper limit is the industry's capacity to pay.

blocks.title: Theories of wage determination
blocks.html:
A union asks for a 10 per cent rise. The employer says the firm cannot afford it. An economist says pay should follow output per worker. Each of the three is using a different theory of what sets wages.

In plain wordsA wage theory is an explanation of why wages stand where they do, and what makes them rise or fall.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a theory of wage determination explains, from stated assumptions, how the level of wages is set.

The theories were built at different times, on different assumptions. Seven are taught, and each captures a part of the truth.

TheoryCredited toMain ideaWhat it gets right, and where it fails
Subsistence wageAssociated with David Ricardo (1817), with Malthus's ideas on population behind itThe wage settles at the "natural price of labour": enough to keep workers alive and their numbers steady.
