If pay rises, more children are born, labour grows plentiful and pay falls back. If pay falls, numbers shrink and pay recovers.Right that plentiful labour keeps pay at the bottom low. Wrong in the long run: real wages in industrial countries rose well above survival level, and families grew smaller as incomes rose.
Wage fundJ. S. Mill (1848), building on Adam Smith and other earlier writersEmployers hold a fixed fund of savings for paying wages. The average wage is the fund divided by the number of workers.Right that capital available for hiring matters. Wrong that the fund is fixed: wages come out of current output. It also implied that unions cannot raise wages in general.
Surplus valueKarl Marx (Capital, 1867)Labour power is bought like any other commodity, at about the cost of keeping the worker going. A worker adds more value in a day than the wage replaces, and the employer keeps the surplus.Right that it puts the split of output between labour and capital at the centre. It rests on a labour theory of value that mainstream economics does not accept.
Residual claimantFrancis A. Walker (1876)Output is shared among land, labour, capital and enterprise. Rent, interest and profit are settled first, and wages are what remains.Right that wages depend on total output, so productivity feeds pay. It gives no reason why labour should come last, or how the others are fixed.
Marginal productivityJ. B. Clark and Philip Wicksteed (1890s)A firm hires workers until the value of the last worker's extra output equals the wage. In a competitive market, the wage equals that value.Right that pay and productivity are linked, and that firms hire fewer people at a higher wage. It assumes competitive markets and similar workers, and it is hard to apply to teamwork.
BargainingJohn Davidson (1898)The wage settles between the most the employer will pay and the least the workers will accept. Bargaining strength decides where: a strong union pulls it up, a strong employer pulls it down.Right that unions and power matter, and it explains why similar workers earn different pay. It gives a range, not a figure, and strength is hard to measure.
BehaviouralBehavioural scientists; Elliott Jaques's "felt-fair pay" is the best knownPay is shaped by what people see as fair, by comparison with others, and by the status, size and prestige of the firm and the employer's concern for staff.Right that a rise can disappoint if a colleague gets more. It lists influences but offers no formula to predict a wage.

Four of them in numbers. These are illustrations.

  • Wage fund. A fund of ₹60 lakh a month pays 300 workers: ₹20,000 each. If 400 workers share the same fund, the average falls to ₹15,000.
  • Residual claimant. Output is worth ₹10 crore. Rent takes ₹1 crore, interest ₹1.5 crore and profit ₹2 crore. Wages are what remains: 10 − (1 + 1.5 + 2) = ₹5.5 crore.
  • Surplus value. A worker adds ₹1,600 of new value in an 8-hour day, or ₹200 an hour. A wage of ₹600 replaces 3 hours of that value. The other 5 hours, worth ₹1,000, are surplus.
  • Marginal productivity. A tailoring unit can add tailors, but each extra tailor adds less output than the one before. Values of the extra output are shown below.

At a wage of ₹600 the unit hires four tailors, since the fourth adds ₹650. Together they bring in 1,500 + 1,100 + 800 + 650 = ₹4,050 and cost 4 × 600 = ₹2,400. If the going wage fell to ₹480, the fifth, who adds ₹500, would be worth hiring too.

Don't confuse the iron law of wages with Ricardo's own words. Ricardo wrote of the "natural price of labour". The name "iron law of wages" was popularised later by the German socialist Ferdinand Lassalle for the same idea. Exam papers often attach the name to Ricardo, so know both.

Don't confuse the wage fund with the residual claimant. In the wage fund theory the wage bill is fixed first and then divided. In the residual claimant theory the wage is what is left after the other factors are paid.

Where it breaks. No single theory explains wages. Subsistence and wage fund describe a poor economy with plentiful labour. Marginal productivity describes what a competitive employer will pay. Bargaining and behavioural theories describe the human side. In practice, market rates and productivity set a range, and bargaining and fairness decide where in it a wage lands. The law of minimum wages then sets a floor that no theory can push below.

For exams. Match each theory to its name. Ricardo goes with subsistence, Mill with the wage fund, Marx with surplus value and Walker with the residual claimant. Clark and Wicksteed go with marginal productivity, Davidson with bargaining, and Jaques with the behavioural view.

Go deeper for practitioners

Mill changed his mind. In 1869 Mill gave up the wage fund doctrine, after criticism by W. T. Thornton. The fund is not set aside in advance; employers pay wages out of what current production brings in. Textbooks still teach the theory because it was so influential.

Jaques's idea. Elliott Jaques proposed that the level of a job can be measured by its "time-span of discretion": how long a person can work before a manager checks the quality of the work. He reported that people in a firm tend to agree on a fair pay for a given time-span. The idea is influential, but it has proved hard to measure and to apply.

A decision. In the tailoring unit, the union asks for ₹700. At ₹700 the third tailor (₹800) is still worth hiring, but the fourth (₹650) is not. Marginal productivity predicts three tailors, whose output is worth 1,500 + 1,100 + 800 = ₹3,400 against a wage bill of 3 × 700 = ₹2,100. The bargaining view says the union may still win ₹700 if the firm's profit can bear it. The better your evidence on the fourth tailor's real contribution, the stronger your reply.

Links. Bargaining is taken further in Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining. Fair pay connects to Adams's equity theory in Organisational Justice and Whistleblowing.

blocks.title: Profit sharing
blocks.html:
An auto-parts firm in Pune has a very good year. The machinists who worked hard see nothing extra. In a poor year their pay would not fall either. Profit sharing ties part of pay to the firm's results, by a rule agreed in advance.

In plain wordsProfit sharing gives employees a pre-agreed share of the firm's profit, on top of their regular wages.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: profit sharing is an agreement, freely entered into, by which employees receive a share, fixed in advance, of the profits.

Three features matter. The payment is in addition to regular wages. The share is a definite percentage of profit, so it bears a fixed relationship to profit. And the rule is agreed on a continuing basis. A profit-linked payment that the employer decides afresh each year does not count.

A worked example. As an illustration, the Pune firm agrees that 10 per cent of each year's profit goes to employees. The yearly wage bill is ₹2 crore.

  • Good year. Profit is ₹80 lakh. The pool is 10% of 80 lakh = ₹8 lakh, which is 4% of the ₹2 crore wage bill. An operator earning ₹3 lakh a year receives 4% of ₹3 lakh = ₹12,000.
  • Poor year. Profit is ₹30 lakh. The pool is ₹3 lakh, or 1.5% of wages. The same operator receives ₹4,500.
  • Loss. There is no pool. Regular wages are untouched.

How profit is paid out. There are three forms.

FormHow it works
Cash (current)Paid in money soon after the year's accounts are closed
Company sharesPaid as shares of the company, so employees become part-owners
DeferredCredited to an account, such as a retirement fund, and paid out at retirement or after a set number of years

Bases of distribution. The pool must also be divided. Common bases are years of service, a fixed percentage of each person's wages in the period (the basis used in the example), merit rating, attendance, performance record, and general record. A firm may mix two or more.

How it differs from a bonus.

PointProfit sharingBonus
Who sets the ruleAgreement between employer and employees, in advanceThe employer, a custom or festival, or the law
What it depends onProfit, by a fixed percentageProfit, output, service or occasion; the amount may be decided afterwards
What employees can count onThe rule, not the amountOften only the custom, unless the law fixes it

Don't confuse profit sharing with ownership, or with statutory bonus. Profit sharing paid in cash gives no ownership; only the share form does. Bonus required by law, which in India is also linked to an establishment's profit, follows rules set by the law, not by an agreement. The Code on Wages, 2019 now carries those rules, and older exam papers use the name Payment of Bonus Act, 1965.

Where it breaks. In a large firm, one machinist's effort barely moves profit, so the link between effort and reward is weak and some may ride on others. Profit also depends on prices, demand and management decisions that workers do not control. In a poor year there is no payout, which can sour the mood. Workers may also doubt how profit is calculated, so honest, open accounts matter. Unions sometimes fear that profit sharing will be used to avoid a wage rise.

In practice. Profit sharing works best as a supplement to fair regular wages and other incentives, never as a replacement. Its main gains are a sense of shared interest, more cooperation and, in some firms, lower turnover. For the employer, part of the labour cost then moves with profit.

For exams. Know the definition, the three features, the forms (cash, shares, deferred), the bases of distribution, and the difference from a bonus.

blocks.title: Taylor, Merrick and Bedaux plans
blocks.html:
Two machinists in the Pune plant differ by one piece in a day: 39 against 40. Under Taylor's plan their pay differs by ₹440. How sharp such a jump should be is the main design choice in a piece-rate plan.

In plain wordsPayment by results links pay to what a worker produces, or to the time saved against a standard, not only to hours at work.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: incentives are variable rewards granted according to the level of achievement of specific results. They are payment for performance, or payment by results.

Individual plans are either time-based, paying a bonus for time saved against a standard time, or piece-based, paying for each unit made against a standard output. The Halsey, Rowan, Emerson and Gantt plans are worked in Compensation Management. Here are three more.

PlanBased onThe ruleGuaranteed wage?
Taylor's differential piece rate (F. W. Taylor)Pieces made, against a standard output set by time studyTwo rates per piece: a higher one at or above the standard, a lower one below itNo
Merrick's multiple piece ratePieces made, as a percentage of standard outputThree rates: the basic rate below 83% of standard; 110% of it from 83% to 100%; 120% of it above 100%No
Bedaux plan (Charles Bedaux)Time saved, counted in "B" pointsTime wage for the time taken, plus 75% of the value of the time savedYes

Taylor and Merrick side by side. Taylor's rule is explained in Theories of Management, so take it as given. As an illustration, the plant sets a standard of 40 pieces a day. Taylor's plan pays ₹50 a piece, on every piece, at or above the standard and ₹40 below it. Merrick's plan takes ₹40 as the basic rate, so the middle rate is 110% of 40 = ₹44 and the top rate is 120% of 40 = ₹48. At 83% of standard a worker has made 33.2 pieces, so 34 pieces is the first whole-number output in the middle band.

Pieces madeShare of standardTaylor payMerrick pay
3075%30 × 40 = ₹1,20030 × 40 = ₹1,200
3382.5%33 × 40 = ₹1,32033 × 40 = ₹1,320
3485%34 × 40 = ₹1,36034 × 44 = ₹1,496
3997.5%39 × 40 = ₹1,56039 × 44 = ₹1,716
40100%40 × 50 = ₹2,00040 × 44 = ₹1,760
41102.5%41 × 50 = ₹2,05041 × 48 = ₹1,968
45112.5%45 × 50 = ₹2,25045 × 48 = ₹2,160

Taylor's jump from 39 to 40 pieces is ₹440, a rise of about 28 per cent. Merrick's two jumps are ₹176 (33 to 34 pieces, about 13 per cent) and ₹208 (40 to 41 pieces, about 12 per cent). So Merrick softens the cliff and rewards the worker who is nearly at standard. But every worker below 83% earns the same rate, whether at 20% or at 82%.

The Bedaux plan. Charles Bedaux fixed standard times by work study and counted them in B points. In the textbook account, one B is a minute of work at normal pace, including an allowance for rest, so 60 B's make a standard hour. The worker is paid for the hours actually taken, plus 75% of the value of the time saved. The other 25% is described as going to the foreman.

Earnings = T × R + 75% × (S − T) × R

Here T is the time taken, S the standard time and R the hourly rate. Take S = 360 B's (6 hours), T = 5 hours and R = ₹10.

  • Time wage: 5 × 10 = ₹50.
  • Time saved: 360 − 300 = 60 B's, which is 1 hour. Its value is 1 × 10 = ₹10.
  • Worker's share: 75% × 10 = ₹7.50.
  • Earnings: 50 + 7.50 = ₹57.50. A worker who takes 7 hours is still paid 7 × 10 = ₹70, with no penalty.

Don't confuse Bedaux with Halsey, and don't start from standard time. Bedaux has the same shape as Halsey's plan, but the worker's share is 75%, not 50%, and the standard is counted in B points. A common slip is to pay for the standard time (6 × 10 = ₹60) and then add the bonus, giving ₹67.50. That pays the saved hour twice. The base is always the time actually taken.

Where it breaks. Taylor's plan has no guaranteed wage and a sharp jump at the standard, which creates stress and treats workers as machines. Merrick's plan is gentler but still pays the same low rate to all who fall below 83%. Bedaux points are complicated, and workers who cannot check the calculation may suspect it, which invites disputes. All three depend on a fair standard, set by work study. Quality and safety need inspection when pay rewards speed.

For exams. Know the rates of Merrick's plan (basic, 110%, 120%, with the 83% and 100% cut-offs), that Taylor and Merrick give no guaranteed wage, and the Bedaux formula with its 75% share.

Go deeper for practitioners

What the jump costs. A straight piece rate of ₹40 pays 40 × 40 = ₹1,600 for 40 pieces. Taylor's plan pays ₹2,000 for the same output, ₹400 or 25 per cent more. That premium is the incentive, and it is also the employer's cost per piece at standard (₹50 against ₹40).

A decision. A new jig lets every machinist reach 45 pieces easily. Under Taylor's plan pay rises from ₹2,000 to 45 × 50 = ₹2,250, though effort has not changed. Re-timing the job to a standard of 45 would pay 45 × 40 = ₹1,800 for the same output, saving ₹450 a day but feeling like a pay cut. The fix is to re-time the standard and to agree the change with the workers first.

Links. Taylor's time and motion studies belong to scientific management, in Theories of Management (Unit 1).

blocks.title: Group incentive plans
blocks.html:
On a bottling line no single worker makes the output; the line does. Individual standards cannot be set, so the bonus has to follow the group's result.

In plain wordsA group incentive plan pays one bonus pool to a whole team, department or plant, for a result they produce together.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: under a group incentive plan, a group bonus is given in place of an individual bonus, and it is shared among the members of the group.

Three group plans are taught. They differ in what the group's result is measured by.

PlanWhat is measuredHow the bonus works
Priestman's planOutput of the whole group, against a standard outputIn the textbook formula, bonus as a percentage of wages equals the percentage increase in output over the standard. Below standard, no bonus.
Scanlon plan (Joseph Scanlon, a union leader of the 1930s)Labour cost as a share of the sales value of output, against a norm from past recordsWhen labour cost falls below the norm, the saving is shared between employees and the company by an agreed split. Production committees collect employees' suggestions.
Profit sharingProfitAn agreed share of profit. Worked in the concept Profit Sharing.

Priestman, worked. As an illustration, a plant's standard is 2,000 units a month and it makes 2,300. The increase is 300 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 15%. Each worker's bonus is 15% of wages. A worker on ₹20,000 a month receives 15% × 20,000 = ₹3,000. If the plant makes 1,900 units, there is no bonus.

Scanlon, worked. As an illustration, the norm is that labour cost equals 30% of the sales value of output. In a month the sales value is ₹1 crore, so the allowed labour cost is 30% × 1 crore = ₹30 lakh. Actual labour cost is ₹27 lakh, a saving of ₹3 lakh. With a 75:25 split in favour of employees, they receive ₹2.25 lakh and the company keeps ₹75,000. Shared equally among 150 employees, that is ₹1,500 each. A saving can come from fewer mistakes and less waste, not only from higher output.

Don't confuse Priestman's plan with Scanlon's. Priestman's plan looks at output against a standard. The Scanlon plan looks at labour cost against sales value, and relies on employees' suggestions. It is not simply "1 per cent bonus for 1 per cent more output".

Where it breaks. A group bonus weakens the link between one person's effort and their pay, so some may ride on others. This is the social loafing described in Group Behaviour, Teams and Leadership. Pressure from co-workers can offset it, but also breed resentment. The Scanlon ratio shifts if prices or the product mix change, so the norm has to be reviewed. Both plans depend on trust, and on figures that employees can see and check.

In practice. Choose an individual plan when each person's output can be measured and the work is separate. Choose a group plan when the work is a chain and cooperation matters more than speed at one station. Group plans also suit firms that want to invite ideas on how to cut waste.

For exams. Match each group plan to its measure: Priestman to output, Scanlon to the labour-cost ratio with employee suggestions, and profit sharing to profit.

chapters.title: International Human Resource Management
chapters.scope: What international HRM is and how it differs from domestic HRM, the three kinds of international employee and Morgan's model, the four staffing approaches, expatriates (their roles, the assignment cycle and why assignments fail) and repatriation.

blocks.title: Meaning of IHRM
blocks.html:
An Indian IT firm opens an office in Munich. HR must now hire under German labour rules, pay engineers posted from India, explain German workplace habits to them, and plan their return home. A firm that works only in Pune never faces this. International HRM is the name for the wider job.

In plain wordsInternational HRM is managing people when one firm works in several countries, so that staff with different nationalities, laws and customs still serve one organisation.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: international human resource management (IHRM) is the set of HR activities a firm carries out at the international level. Its aim is to meet the firm's objectives and to gain an advantage over competitors at home and abroad. It covers the usual HR functions across borders, plus extra work such as expatriate management.

IHRM is mostly the concern of a multinational company (MNC): a firm that owns and runs operations in more than one country. The country where its head office stands is the home (or parent) country. A country where it runs a branch or subsidiary is a host country.

The functions are the ones covered in Human Resource Management (this unit): recruitment, selection, training and development, appraisal and, when needed, dismissal. IHRM does them across borders. It adds work that a domestic firm never needs, such as choosing, preparing and paying people for foreign postings, and bringing them home again.

Back to Munich. In Pune, the firm deals with one set of labour laws, one tax system and one set of workplace habits. In Munich it deals with German law and German customs, while the engineers it sends bring Indian expectations about pay and career. The table shows how far the job widens.

BasisDomestic HRMInternational HRM
ScopeInside one countryBetween two or more countries
EmployeesMainly one nationalitySeveral nationalities, sorted into PCNs, HCNs and TCNs (the next concept)
ActivitiesThe standard HR functionsThe same functions, plus relocation, expatriate pay and tax, cross-cultural training and language help
EnvironmentOne legal, economic and cultural systemSeveral systems; laws, politics, exchange rates and cultural distance all matter
Personal livesThe firm deals mainly with the employeeThe firm often deals with the family too: housing, schooling, the partner's job
RiskLowerHigher: a failed posting, a political event or a currency swing can be costly

The objectives of IHRM. A firm that does IHRM well aims to:

  • build the managerial, technical and knowledge skills of its managers and staff, so that it can run global operations;
  • manage the performance, pay and career path of staff who work abroad;
  • organise cross-cultural counselling and language training;
  • understand work practices in different countries, and bring them closer together;
  • build HR strategies, and new ways of managing performance, that stand up against global competitors;
  • reduce cultural friction and build harmony between people of different cultures.

Don't confuse IHRM with comparative HRM. IHRM manages the people of one firm that operates across borders. Comparative HRM compares how HR is practised in different countries, for example how Indian and German firms hire.

Where it breaks. The line between domestic and international is not sharp. A bank in India that employs staff from many states and languages already meets some of these problems (see Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour, this unit). What changes abroad is that laws, currencies and governments change as well.

For exams. A matching question has paired international HRM with managing the human resource challenges of international operations. Learn the differences in the table and the objectives as a list.

More countries, more kinds of staff, more activities, more risk.

blocks.title: Employee types and Morgan's model
blocks.html:
The Munich office has three engineers. One was sent from Pune, one was hired in Munich, and one came from the firm's office in Poland. Their pay, tax, rights and career paths differ. IHRM first sorts such people by nationality.

In plain wordsIHRM sorts international staff by comparing a person's nationality with two countries: the one where the head office stands, and the one where the person works.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a parent country national (PCN) is a citizen of the country where the firm's head office stands. A host country national (HCN) is a citizen of the country where a subsidiary operates. A third country national (TCN) is a citizen of neither. PCNs are also called home country employees.

Two illustrations follow: the Indian IT firm's Munich office, and a European carmaker, headquartered in Germany, with a plant in Pune. Both firms are hypothetical.

TypeMeaningIndian IT firm's Munich officeCarmaker's Pune plant
PCNCitizen of the head-office country; may work at head office or be posted abroadAn Indian engineer posted from Pune to MunichA German engineer posted from head office to Pune
HCNCitizen of the country where the unit operatesA German engineer hired in MunichAn Indian engineer hired at the Pune plant
TCNCitizen of neither countryA Polish team lead from the firm's office in PolandA Spanish engineer sent from the carmaker's plant in Spain

The label depends on the firm and the unit, not on the person alone. An Indian engineer at the carmaker's Pune plant is an HCN. If the carmaker sends her to its plant in Spain, she is a TCN there. If she works for the Indian IT firm in Munich, she is a PCN.

Don't confuse where a person works with which type she is. An Indian working abroad is not automatically a host country national. The host country is the one where the unit stands, so an HCN is a national of that country. Nor are PCNs only the people at head office: those posted abroad are PCNs too, and they are the expatriates described later in this chapter.

Morgan's model. P. V. Morgan (1986) set out a three-dimensional model of what IHRM covers. It joins three sets of three things.

  • Three broad HR activities: procurement (getting people), allocation (placing them in jobs and units) and utilisation (getting good work from them). The everyday tasks, such as planning, recruitment, selection, training, appraisal and pay, sit under these headings.
  • Three country categories: the home country, the host country, and other countries that may supply labour or finance.
  • Three types of employee: PCNs, HCNs and TCNs.

Two combinations show how the cube works. Hiring local engineers in Munich is procurement of HCNs in the host country. Posting an engineer from Pune to Munich is allocation of a PCN from the home country to the host country.

Don't confuse Morgan's HR activities with the list of HR functions. Study notes sometimes give recruitment, training, appraisal and compensation as Morgan's first dimension. Those are examples of the work. Morgan's three broad headings are procurement, allocation and utilisation.

Where it breaks. Nationality is a blunt label. A person with two passports, or one who has lived in the host country for twenty years, fits no box neatly. The model also describes what IHRM covers. It does not tell a firm whom to send where; the staffing approaches (next concept) do that.

For exams. Know the three dimensions in order: activities, countries, employees.

ACE: Activities, Countries, Employees. Each has three parts.

blocks.title: Staffing approaches
blocks.html:
The new Munich office needs a head. The firm could send a manager from Pune, hire a German locally, or pick the best candidate from any of its offices. Each choice trades control, cost and local knowledge. Four staffing approaches name the options.

In plain wordsA staffing approach is a firm's general rule for who fills the key posts in its foreign units: its own nationals, local nationals, or the best people from anywhere.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: Howard Perlmutter (1969) classified the orientation of a multinational's top management as ethnocentric (home-country), polycentric (host-country) and geocentric (world-oriented). A fourth, regiocentric (region-oriented), was added in later work. In staffing, they decide whether key posts go to PCNs, to HCNs, to the best person of any nationality, or to people from the same region.

ApproachKey posts and controlAdvantagesDisadvantages
EthnocentricKey posts at head office and in subsidiaries go to PCNs. Head office takes the main decisions; subsidiaries have little autonomy.Tight control and fit with head office. The parent's methods transfer easily. It works when no local managers are ready.Local staff see no route to the top, so morale and retention suffer. PCNs cost more, need time to adapt, and may apply head-office habits that do not suit the place.
PolycentricEach subsidiary is treated as a distinct national unit and run by HCNs. PCNs hold the key posts at head office. Subsidiaries have more local autonomy, not less.Local language, law and market knowledge. No expatriate cost or adjustment problems. Continuity of management.Head office and subsidiaries drift apart. HCNs rarely reach head office, so careers stay local. Learning is hard to share across units.
GeocentricKey posts anywhere, head office included, go to the best person, whether PCN, HCN or TCN. Head office and subsidiaries work as one global network.Best use of talent. It builds a pool of international managers and a global outlook.Costly and slow: relocation, training and a complex pay structure. Immigration and work-permit rules can block moves. It needs strong central planning.
RegiocentricKey posts go to managers from the same geographic region as the unit, such as South Asia or Europe. Staff move within the region, but seldom to head office.More local feel than posting people from far away, at lower cost than global moves.The region can become its own silo, with a regional view in place of a global one. Careers stop at the regional border.

When each suits.

  • Ethnocentric: a new market where the firm has no local managers yet, or where it wants its own methods copied exactly. The carmaker's first years in Pune, when engineers from head office set up the plant, fit this.
  • Polycentric: a market that differs sharply from home, where local knowledge decides success. The same plant, years later, dealing with Indian suppliers, dealers and labour law through Indian managers, fits this.
  • Geocentric: a mature firm with a global strategy, where talent and ideas must flow across units. A large IT firm staffing a Munich project with whoever has the right skills, from any office, fits this.
  • Regiocentric: a firm organised by region, whose neighbouring countries share markets and languages. An IT firm that staffs its European operations with managers from several European offices fits this.

Don't confuse polycentric with ethnocentric. In ethnocentric staffing head office keeps control and subsidiaries have little autonomy. In polycentric staffing the subsidiary is run by local nationals and has more autonomy. Do not confuse regiocentric with geocentric either: regiocentric picks from one region, geocentric from the whole world.

Ethno: home. Poly: host. Geo: best anywhere. Regio: the region.

Where it breaks. These are ideal types. Most firms mix them: PCNs for finance, HCNs for sales, a TCN for a technical post. They also change over time, and many firms begin ethnocentric and become more polycentric as they learn a market. Nationality is only a stand-in for what the post needs, which is skill and fit.

For exams. Match each approach to who fills the key posts, and give one advantage and one disadvantage of each. A common slip is to say that polycentric subsidiaries have little autonomy.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. The carmaker's Pune plant is run by a German quality head, a PCN who leaves in eighteen months. An Indian deputy is capable but has never worked with head-office systems. Do you name her successor now, send her to head office for a year first, or advertise for another PCN? Naming her early keeps local talent and cuts cost, but quality control may weaken meanwhile. A year at head office closes much of the gap.

Finer point. Perlmutter described top management's attitude across many areas of a multinational, not only staffing. Staffing is one place where the attitude shows.

Links. Strategic Human Resource Management (this unit) explains why staffing should fit the strategy. Career Planning and Development (this unit) covers succession planning, which is what the decision above needs.

blocks.title: Expatriates and their assignments
blocks.html:
A European carmaker sends an engineer to set up its Pune plant. She is paid more than local staff, her partner must find work, her child needs a school, and in three years she must return to a job that may not exist. Expatriate management is the part of IHRM that handles all this.

In plain wordsAn expatriate is an employee whom the firm sends to work in a country that is not their own.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: expatriates are employees of an organisation in one country who are assigned to work in another country on long-term or short-term business projects.

Firms send them to set up operations, to enter overseas markets, and to pass skills and knowledge to their business partners. The experience also builds the firm's pool of managers who can succeed in a global market. Both PCNs and TCNs can be expatriates. An HCN working in her own country is not.

Six strategic roles. An expatriate does more than fill a post. Textbooks describe six roles; one person often plays several. The third column shows each for a manager sent from Pune to the Indian IT firm's Munich office (an illustration).

RoleWhat the expatriate doesIn Munich
Agent of direct controlMakes sure the unit follows head-office policy, by direct supervision. This is formal, rule-based control.Signs off bids and checks that data-security rules are kept
Agent of socialisationPasses on the firm's values and way of working. This is informal control through shared beliefs.Shows new German hires how the firm treats clients and quality, by working beside them
Network builderBuilds personal links between the unit, head office and other units. The links carry information and informal control.Knows people in Pune and elsewhere, and quickly connects a German team with the right specialist
Transfer of competence and knowledgeMoves skills and common work practices into the unit, and often brings local knowledge back.Trains the Munich team in the firm's delivery methods and learns what German clients expect
Boundary spannerLinks the firm to its outside world: gathers market information and represents the firm to clients, officials and business groups.Meets contacts at a trade event in Munich and reports a client's plans home
Language nodeSpeaks both the corporate language (often English) and the local one, so messages between head office and unit pass through the person.The manager who knows German becomes the person both sides turn to for translation

Control, socialise, network, transfer, span, speak.

Don't confuse the two kinds of control. The agent of direct control watches and checks, with rules and supervision. The agent of socialisation shapes what people want, by sharing values. Also, an expatriate is not an immigrant: the employer sends her, usually for a set period, and expects her back or on to the next post.

The assignment cycle. An expatriate assignment is a managed sequence, not a single transfer.

  • Selection. Technical skill is necessary but not enough. Firms also look for adaptability, openness to other cultures, communication skills, and a family ready to move.
  • Preparation. A briefing on the job and the place, language lessons, and cross-cultural training (see Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour, this unit), ideally with a visit to the host city first.
  • Compensation. Most firms use the balance-sheet approach. The aim is that the expatriate keeps the standard of living she had at home. The firm compares her costs at home and in the host country in four groups: income tax, housing, goods and services, and savings. It pays the gaps, then adds an incentive for going and allowances for hard postings.
  • Support. Help with housing, schooling and the partner's work, and a contact at head office who keeps her in touch.
  • Performance review. The host manager sees the work but may not know head-office goals. The home manager knows the goals but does not see the work. A fair review uses both and allows for the host setting.

Why assignments fail. A failed assignment is one that ends early or falls far short. Research since the early 1980s often names the family's difficulty in adjusting, especially the partner's, among the most common reasons. Others are the expatriate's own difficulty with the culture, personal problems, inability to cope with bigger responsibility, poor selection and weak preparation or support.

Where it breaks. Popular figures for how often assignments fail are often high but rest on weak evidence, and they depend on how failure is defined. Long postings are also costly, so many firms now use shorter assignments, regular commuting or virtual teams where the job allows.

In practice. Before sending someone, ask whether a local hire or a short visit can do the job. An expatriate package usually costs much more than a local salary. If an expatriate is the answer, spend on selection, preparation and support, because that is where failures start.

For exams. Know the six roles by name, the assignment steps in order, and what the balance-sheet approach tries to do.

blocks.title: Repatriation
blocks.html:
After three years in Munich, an engineer returns to Pune. Her old post has been filled, her team has changed, and her manager has no idea what she learned. Friends say she has become a bit foreign. Within a year she resigns. The firm paid to send her abroad and lost what she learned on the way back.

In plain wordsRepatriation is bringing an expatriate home at the end of an assignment, and helping her settle back into home life and the home organisation.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: repatriation is the process of an expatriate returning to the home country after an international assignment is complete, or after it ends for some other reason.

The return is the last step of the assignment cycle, and one that firms often neglect. Repatriation has four stages. They are the firm's tasks, in order. The first three are practical; the fourth is personal and professional, and it can last long after the paperwork ends.

StageWhat happensWhat goes wrong, and what helps
1 PreparationPlans for the future are made. The expatriate learns about the post she will take at home.With no post agreed, she returns without a role. Settle the next job before she leaves the host country.
2 Physical relocationHer belongings are removed, ties with colleagues and friends are broken, and she travels home.Without good relocation help, a practical task becomes a source of stress.
3 TransitionThe firm arranges temporary housing, the family's house and school, and the formalities.Gaps in housing or school places strain the family at the worst moment.
4 ReadjustmentShe settles back into home life and the home firm. Reverse culture shock and career concerns appear.The two cultures may differ greatly; the role, status and pay may be lower than abroad.

Reverse culture shock is the stress of coming home to a place that has changed, and of being a changed person. It surprises people because they expect home to be easy. Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour (this unit) explains culture shock and its reverse. The career side is just as hard. Abroad she may have had more responsibility and independence. At home she may find no suitable post, lower status, pay that falls when the foreign allowances stop, and colleagues who never ask what she learned.

Keeping the returnee's knowledge. What she knows about the host market, the people and the working methods is the return on the whole assignment. Firms can protect it in five ways:

  • agree her next post before she leaves the host country;
  • keep a mentor at head office in touch with her during the assignment;
  • hold a debriefing on her return, and record what she learned;
  • give her work that uses the new skills, such as leading a project with the foreign unit;
  • ask her to brief and train the next expatriate.

Cultural distance. How far apart the home and host cultures are shapes every stage, from selection to readjustment. Hofstede's dimensions, taught in Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour (this unit), give the common words for that distance.

Don't confuse the four repatriation stages with the stages of culture shock. The U-curve (honeymoon, crisis, adjustment, mastery) describes how a person feels over time. The four repatriation stages are the firm's tasks in bringing her home. The word "readjustment" appears in both ideas, which is why they are often mixed up.

Where it breaks. The four stages are a tidy sequence; real returns overlap them. The firm's tasks can be finished while the person is still struggling, and families do not follow one timetable. Readjustment is often harder where the home and host cultures differ greatly.

In practice. Treat the return as a career-planning decision, not a travel arrangement. A six-month countdown with a named owner in HR, a confirmed post and a debriefing date helps prevent many of the problems above.

For exams. Give the four stages in order and say what happens in each. Reverse culture shock belongs to the last stage.

Go deeper for practitioners

The W-curve. John and Jeanne Gullahorn (1963) extended the U-curve into a W: a second dip in feeling on return, followed by a second recovery. Like the U-curve, it has only mixed support in research, so use it as a warning, not as a timetable.

A decision. A returnee asks to join a Pune client project that needs her German experience. Her former manager wants her back in the old team, which is short-staffed. If you send her back to the old team, it gets help at once. If you give her the project, you use the knowledge that the posting paid for. Which costs more if you get it wrong, and what would you promise her about her next move?

Links. Career Planning and Development (this unit) treats the return as a career move. Human Resource Planning (this unit) shows how to count the returnees coming back when you forecast posts.
